turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: ... early days, it's very important to just go back to the basics, build the skeleton before you put on the makeup. So the first question I would ask is, do you have a website? Is it fast? Do the search engine knows that it exists? Okay, great. The next step would be, can people find it? If they can't find it, do you need to write content to make sure that people can find it? Only after all of those questions are answered, should you then consider, do I have money? Can I put it behind some paid ads to make sure people come to my website? You can't run a successful paid ads program if you have a website that's loading in four plus seconds. So really going back to the basics and starting from a good experience at the core and then expanding step-by-step from there.
turns.zh: ……在早期阶段，回归基础非常重要——先搭好骨架，再化妆打扮。所以我会先问的第一个问题是：你有网站吗？它快吗？搜索引擎知道它的存在吗？好的，很棒。下一步就是，人们能找到它吗？如果找不到，你是否需要写一些内容来确保人们能找到它？只有把这些问题都回答完了，你才应该考虑：我有钱吗？我能不能把它放到付费广告后面，来确保人们访问我的网站？如果你的网站加载需要四秒以上，你就没法跑一个成功的付费广告项目。所以真的要回归基础，从一个好的核心体验开始，然后再一步步地向外扩展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Welcome to Lenny's Podcast where I interview world-class product leaders and growth experts to learn from their hard won experiences building and growing today's most successful products. Today my guest is Meltem Kuran Berkowitz. Meltem is head of growth at Deel, which is arguably the fastest growing SaaS business of all time, possibly even faster than Ramp, which we delved into in a previous episode. They went from $0 in revenue to a mind-boggling $300 million in revenue in three years, while also staying EBITDA positive.
turns.zh: 欢迎来到 Lenny 的播客，在这里我会采访世界一流的产品负责人和增长专家，从他们打造和增长当今最成功产品的亲身经历中学习。今天的嘉宾是 Meltem Kuran Berkowitz。Meltem 是 Deel 的增长负责人，Deel 可以说是有史以来增长最快的 SaaS 业务，甚至可能比我们上一期深入探讨过的 Ramp 还要快。他们在三年内从 0 收入增长到令人难以置信的 3 亿美元收入，同时还保持着 EBITDA 为正。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Meltem has led their growth team from the early days. And today leads all their growth efforts, including paid ads, product marketing, content, community, brand and more. Before joining Deel, she was leading marketing efforts at Bench Accounting. In our conversation, Meltem shares how Deel kick started growth through low-cost growth channels like tapping into communities like Reddit and also content and SEO. She also talks about how she evolved her thinking on growth investments as the company grew. She shares a bunch of tactical advice for how to do SEO well, how to do paid ads well, and how to structure your early growth team and prioritize your early investments. She also shares her experience building a culture of speed and optimism and so much more. Enjoy this episode with Meltem Kuran Berkowitz after a short word from our sponsors.
turns.zh: Meltem 从早期就开始领导他们的增长团队。如今她负责所有的增长工作，包括付费广告、产品营销、内容、社区、品牌等等。在加入 Deel 之前，她在 Bench Accounting 领导营销工作。在我们的对话中，Meltem 分享了 Deel 如何通过 Reddit 这类社区以及内容、SEO 等低成本增长渠道来启动增长。她还谈到了随着公司成长，她对增长投资的思考是如何演变的。她分享了大量关于如何做好 SEO、如何做好付费广告，以及如何搭建早期增长团队、确定早期投资优先级的战术建议。她还分享了她打造速度与乐观文化的经验，以及更多内容。在听完我们赞助商的简短介绍后，请享受这期与 Meltem Kuran Berkowitz 的节目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Meltem, thank you so much for being here, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: Meltem，非常感谢你能来，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Thank you for having me, I'm very excited to be here.
turns.zh: 谢谢你邀请我，我真的很兴奋能来这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm more excited that you're here. So you're head of growth at Deel. For people that aren't familiar with Deel, can you just give us a sense of what does Deel do briefly? And then also can you just share some stats around the trajectory of Deel? It feels like it's been this extraordinary journey, and I'm curious just to hear some of the stats of just how extraordinary.
turns.zh: 我比你来这里还要兴奋。你是 Deel 的增长负责人。对于不熟悉 Deel 的人，你能简单讲一下 Deel 是做什么的吗？另外，你能分享一些关于 Deel 发展轨迹的数据吗？感觉这是一段非比寻常的旅程，我很好奇能听到一些数据，看看它到底有多惊人。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yeah, so Deel is payroll, HR, and compliance platform for global teams. So essentially we help companies expand globally with tools like Deel HR, immigration, employer record hiring, independent contractor hiring, payroll, both global and US. So whether you're trying to hire someone as a full-time employee in Japan or you're trying to make sure your contractor in Germany has everything they need on day one, our platform allows you to take care of everything all in one place.
turns.zh: 是的，Deel 是面向全球团队的薪酬、人力资源和合规平台。所以本质上我们帮助公司用 Deel HR、移民、雇主记录招聘、独立承包商招聘、薪酬（全球和美国）等工具在全球扩张。所以无论你是想在日本招聘一名全职员工，还是想确保你在德国的承包商在第一天就拥有他们需要的一切，我们的平台都能让你在一个地方搞定所有事情。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And when I joined Deel, actually that was around July, 2020, we were less than a million dollars in ARR. And then over time, within the first year on January, 2021, we were at $4 million ARR. We finished 2021 with 57 million. April '22, we were looking at a hundred million. And then we started off this year with $295 million in ARR. And what we're particularly proud of is that we've been EBITDA positive. So that's something that we are very, very proud of on top of the ARR growth.
turns.zh: 我加入 Deel 的时候，大概是 2020 年 7 月，我们的 ARR 还不到 100 万美元。然后随着时间推移，在第一年内的 2021 年 1 月，我们达到了 400 万美元 ARR。2021 年底我们做到了 5700 万。2022 年 4 月，我们看到了 1 亿。然后今年我们以 2.95 亿美元 ARR 开局。我们特别自豪的是我们一直保持 EBITDA 为正。所以这是我们除了 ARR 增长之外，非常、非常自豪的一件事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And you said that you were super early at Deel. Can you give us a sense of just how early and what that was like?
turns.zh: 太厉害了。你说过你在 Deel 非常早期就加入了。你能大概说一下到底有多早，当时是什么样子吗？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: I was the second hire to the marketing team, and I was I believe either employee 19 or 20 on the overall Deel team.
turns.zh: 我是营销团队的第二号 hires（招聘），我相信我是整个 Deel 团队的第 19 或第 20 号员工。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We had the head of product from Ramp on this podcast, and it feels like there's this little bit of which company grew faster early on in the trajectory of the two, but we don't have to debate it. It feels like these are maybe the two fastest growing SaaS businesses in history. Does that sound about right?
turns.zh: 我们请过 Ramp 的负责人上这个播客，感觉这两家公司早期谁增长更快有点争论，不过我们不必去辩论它。感觉它们可能是历史上增长最快的两家 SaaS 公司。这么说对吗？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: That's true, yeah. So Ramp was the first one to be crowned the fastest growing, and then we took that crown from them. So I think we're both right, in that at a certain point in time we've each been the fastest growing. But they're amazing.
turns.zh: 没错，是的。Ramp 是最先被冠以"增长最快"称号的，然后我们从他们手里夺过了这个桂冠。所以我觉得我们都没错，因为在某个时间点上我们各自都曾是增长最快的。但他们也很了不起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I want to start with is something that I heard about you, which is that you specialize in cheaper growth channels, and that's actually the reason that Deel ended up hiring you, is they wanted to find ways to grow cheaply. And so a couple of questions. One is just, what did you find worked really well from that perspective at Deel? And then two, what are today's maybe cheaper growth channels that you think people are under investing in? Whatever you're willing to share there, I don't know if you want to give away all your secrets.
turns.zh: 我想先从我听说过的关于你的一件事开始，就是你擅长更便宜的增长渠道，而这实际上也是 Deel 最终雇佣你的原因——他们想找到低成本增长的方法。所以有几个问题。第一，从那个角度看，你发现 Deel 身上哪些方法真的很有效？第二，今天有哪些可能被人低估投资的、更便宜的增长渠道？你愿意分享多少都行，我不知道你想不想把你的秘密全说出来。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: I'm happy to give away all and everything. So I think before we dive into the list of cheap channels, which I will get to, it's very important to notice, especially in the B2B world, most of the businesses are started because there's an active problem. And so when you go out to the market and try to answer people's questions, people don't want to be sold to, they want their problem solved. So those cheaper channels are often places where people are just trying to get an answer to their question. So whether that be search engine optimization through the articles that you write for people, looking onto Reddit where people are asking these questions in communities, forming partnerships with other groups that are trying to answer these questions, existing communities where other business leaders are connecting with each other and looking at their peers to find answers to shared problems that they're having, or places like Quora. That's, when you think about cheap channels, that's a really good place to start, is just add value to people, answer their questions.
turns.zh: 我很乐意把一切都分享出来。所以在我们深入那一串便宜渠道（我会讲到的）之前，有一点很重要，尤其是在 B2B 世界里：大多数企业都是因为存在一个切实的问题才成立的。所以当你走向市场、试图回答人们的问题时，人们不想被推销，他们想让自己的问题被解决。所以那些更便宜的渠道，往往就是人们只是想找到某个问题答案的地方。无论是你为人们写的文章来做 SEO，还是去 Reddit 上人们在社区里问这些问题，又或者和其他也在回答这些问题的团体建立合作，还有那些企业领导者彼此联系、向同行寻找共同问题答案的现有社区，或者像 Quora 这样的地方。所以当你想到便宜渠道时，一个很好的起点就是：只是为人们增加价值、回答他们的问题。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And when you answer their questions and present your solution, if it's a fit to what they're looking for, that ends up being a cheap channel for you. You don't necessarily have to advertise, when you go to Reddit and you set up those keywords to be tracking when people ask certain questions, you're not paying any money to do that. You're just seeing, oh, someone has this question, I have the answer to that, here you go. And connecting with them, it takes time. But early on, those were a lot of the things that we invested in.
turns.zh: 当你回答他们的问题并展示你的解决方案时，如果它符合他们要找的东西，那对你来说就变成了一个便宜的渠道。你不一定非得打广告，当你去 Reddit，设置好那些关键词来追踪人们什么时候问某些问题，你做这件事是不花钱的。你只是看到，哦，有人有这个问题，我有那个答案，给你。然后和他们建立联系，这需要时间。但早期，这些就是我们投入的很多事情。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And I think a lot of people jump that because they think, "Oh, it's one person here, two people there." But when you start helping people, that combined with word of mouth, and guess what, these are digital places, you provide one answer and your answer lives out there for other people to repeatedly refine. As long as we're not talking about a closed Slack community, maybe a conversation happening in DMs. So when I think about cheap channels, I think about where are people asking the questions, that might be Google or that might be Reddit or any other channel, and providing them the answers, so they know that your solution exists.
turns.zh: 我觉得很多人会跳过这一步，因为他们想，"哦，这里一个人，那里两个人。"但当你开始帮助人们，再加上口碑传播，而且猜怎么着，这些都是数字化的地方，你提供了一个答案，你的答案就会一直留在那里，供其他人反复参考。只要我们说的不是封闭的 Slack 社区，可能是在私信里发生的对话。所以当我思考便宜渠道时，我想的是人们都在哪里问问题——可能是 Google，也可能是 Reddit 或任何其他渠道——然后给他们答案，让他们知道你的解决方案存在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, this is awesome. So this Reddit example is that, which you actually did, you set alerts for when people have questions about HR hiring internationally I imagine, and then had someone go in there and give them some advice?
turns.zh: 好的，这太棒了。所以这个 Reddit 的例子，也就是你实际做过的：你设置了提醒，当人们对国际化 HR 招聘有问题时——我猜是这样——然后派个人进去给他们一些建议？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yes, exactly that's what we did.
turns.zh: 是的，我们做的正是这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I love that.
turns.zh: 哇，我喜欢这个。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: It's important to notice that if you're looking at a subreddit of about a thousand people, recognize the upper size of this audience, you're not going to win 5,000 businesses through that Reddit community, but you're maybe going to win 10% of the people there that are having this problem. So it's very important when investing in these cheap channels to focus on what's the upper limit of the audience size.
turns.zh: 要注意的是，如果你看一个大约一千人的 subreddit，要认识到这个受众的上限规模，你不可能通过那个 Reddit 社区赢得 5000 家企业，但你大概能赢得那里 10% 正面临这个问题的人。所以在投资这些便宜渠道时，关注受众规模的上限非常重要。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And also I see a lot of people sometimes go blindly into SEO. They're like, "We're just going to write content," which I'm a huge fan of SEO, happy to discuss that later, but if people aren't asking this question to Google, you can write all the content you want, it doesn't matter, nobody's going to find it.
turns.zh: 而且我也看到很多人有时候盲目地去做 SEO。他们说，"我们就写内容吧"——而我是 SEO 的忠实粉丝，很乐意稍后讨论——但如果人们没在 Google 上问这个问题，你写多少内容都没用，没人会找到它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this so much, because it connects with something I find again and again, is one of the more effective early growth channels is tapping into an existing community and piggybacking off of what they've already built. Airbnb is a little bit of an example where they went to Craigslist. Actually most people pull people off Craigslist, Uber pull people off Craigslist, Lyft, so many companies just piggybacked off Craigslist and built up their own company.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了，因为它和我反复发现的一件事相通：更有效的早期增长渠道之一，就是切入一个现有社区，并搭上他们已经建立起来的东西的便车。Airbnb 就是一个小例子，他们去了 Craigslist。实际上大多数人都从 Craigslist 上拉人，Uber 从 Craigslist 拉人，Lyft 也是，这么多公司都搭了 Craigslist 的便车，建立起自己的公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But what you said is so important, which is you can't just go into a community and be like, "Hey, everyone, check out what I've got." You need to add value to people and add value to the community, otherwise no one's going to pay attention to you, they're going to kick you out.
turns.zh: 但你说的很重要的一点，就是你不能只是进到一个社区然后说，"嘿，大家，看看我有什么。"你需要给人们、给社区增加价值，否则没人会理你，他们还会把你踢出去。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so I think that is a really important insight is if you're trying to say piggyback off of a community, the most important thing is you need to add value to the community.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得这是一个非常重要的洞察：如果你想搭某个社区的便车，最重要的是你需要给社区增加价值。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yeah, be someone people actually want to talk to.
turns.zh: 对，要成为人们真正想与之交谈的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Is there a tool that you found for that Reddit strategy of just how to know if someone's talking about hiring say internationally?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。有没有一个你发现的工具，可以用来做那个 Reddit 策略——就是怎么知道某人是不是在谈论比如国际化招聘？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: I did a very janky assistant setup, I'm not proud of it, but it works. Someone else out there built it and I just plugged in the keywords we were looking for into it.
turns.zh: 我搞了一个非常粗糙的助手设置，我对此并不骄傲，但它能用。是别人做出来，然后我把我们要找的关键词插进去的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know it wasn't just Reddit, and I'm curious what else you found was worth your time, but how did you figure out that's where your potential community and potential users were spending time?
turns.zh: 我知道不只是 Reddit，我很好奇你还发现什么值得你花时间，但你是怎么确定那里就是你的潜在社区和潜在用户花时间的地方的？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Well, I think over time Reddit became the place that you go to when you want peer answers, whether that peer is someone right next to you or someone halfway across the world. So it was a very obvious place for me to go to understand, what's top of mind for my audience? But also there are so many subreddits, whether it's founders or HR managers, that people are just asking their community. Because oftentimes they have very specific questions. You can't just ask that to Google because they have one thing that means that they might not be able to qualify for the exact solution that is what's most used out there. So Reddit just became the place over the years for people to ask their specific questions semi-anonymously and get answers from their community, and multiple answers to be able to judge which works better versus didn't. So it was one of the first places that myself and my team went to.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得随着时间推移，Reddit 变成了当你想要同行答案时会去的地方，无论这个同行是你旁边的人，还是半个地球之外的人。所以对我来说，它是一个非常明显的地方，可以让我了解：我的受众最关心什么？而且有那么多 subreddit——无论是创始人还是 HR 经理——人们就在那里问他们的社区。因为他们经常有非常具体的问题。你不能直接去问 Google，因为他们有一个东西意味着他们可能不符合外面最常用解决方案的资格。所以多年来 Reddit 变成了人们半匿名地问自己具体问题、并从社区获得答案，以及获得多个答案以便判断哪个更好、哪个不行的地方。所以它成了我和我的团队最先去的地方之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is this something that worked really well, mostly at the beginning to kickstart growth or how early was this? And then how much of your growth would you say came from this sort of strategy early on?
turns.zh: 这个在启动增长的早期效果真的很好吗，还是说有多早？然后早期你大概有多少增长是来自这类策略？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: I believe I set up that little keyword tracking within the first day of me starting my role at Deel. So it was very, very early. And we still do this by the way. We still provide answers across Reddit, Quora communities. We're still out there connecting with people. Over time, of course, it went from maybe being 15% of our funnel to less than 5% of our funnel because the rest of our funnel has grown a lot. But the next number of people that we get to share our solution with through those channels have continued to grow over time.
turns.zh: 我记得我在 Deel 入职第一天之内就设置好了那个关键词追踪。所以非常非常早。而且顺便说一句，我们至今还在做这件事。我们仍在 Reddit、Quora 社区里提供答案。我们还在外面和人们建立联系。当然，随着时间推移，它从可能占我们漏斗的 15%，降到了不到 5%，因为漏斗的其他部分增长了很多。但通过那些渠道我们分享解决方案的人数，这些年一直在持续增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to something I asked that I want to touch on is, in today's world are there any cheaper growth channels that you are excited about? Or is it essentially the same idea? Look for where your potential users are and ideally asking questions that you could help answer? Is that roughly how you think about it still?
turns.zh: 回到我问过、想再聊一下的一个点：在今天的这个世界里，有没有什么更便宜的增长渠道是让你兴奋的？还是说本质上还是同一个思路——去找你的潜在用户在哪里、ideally 还在问你能帮忙回答的问题？你现在大致还是这么想的吗？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: That is still roughly how I think about it. I would add social channels to that as well. I think Twitter's a great place, people ask questions oftentimes, so there are communities. And when someone has answered that question, other people piggyback off of that. But anywhere where someone is asking a question, I would consider to fall into this category of a cheap channel.
turns.zh: 大体上我还是这么想的。我还会把社交媒体渠道也加进去。我觉得 Twitter 是个好地方，人们经常问问题，所以那里也有社区。当有人回答了那个问题，其他人就会搭便车。但任何有人在问问题的地方，我都会归到便宜渠道这个类别里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's an example of answering a question in a value-add way versus a maybe less effective way in your experience?
turns.zh: 在你看来，一个以"增加价值"的方式回答问题的例子，和一种可能不太有效的方式，分别是什么样的？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: I would say the least effective way would be, "Hey, we've solved that problem, check out our website." Okay, cool, if you have five seconds, do that. But the value-add way would be explaining what the solution to that problem is. Because the reality is there are a lot of people out there who can probably solve this, and then providing your solution, but answer their question first, and then let them decide if they want to come with you or go with someone else. But the whole point of someone asking a question isn't to be sold a solution. It's like, "I just need an answer." So genuinely treat this person like a friend of yours, answer their question, be like, "Yes, it's doable. No, it's not doable. Yes, you can do it, but you need to consider X, Y, Z. If you want to learn more about it, you can chat with us."
turns.zh: 我会说最无效的方式是，"嘿，我们解决了那个问题，来看看我们的网站。"好，如果你有五秒钟，可以这么做。但增加价值的方式，是解释那个问题的解决方案是什么。因为现实是，外面有很多人可能都能解决这个问题，然后你再提供你的方案——但先回答他们的问题，然后让他们自己决定是想跟着你走，还是选别人。但某人问问题的整个目的不是为了被卖一个方案。而是"我只需要一个答案"。所以真诚地把这个人当你的朋友对待，回答他的问题，像这样说，"是的，这能做到。不，这做不到。是的，你能做，但你需要考虑 X、Y、Z。如果你想了解更多，可以和我们聊聊。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And these were people on the team or you answering these questions, it wasn't some automated system?
turns.zh: 而且这些是团队里的人或者你自己回答这些问题，不是什么自动化系统？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: It was never automated. It still isn't today. We would never automate our interactions with people. So early days, it was myself, the other people on my team, our co-founders, which to this day they still do by the way. So it's a lot of people on the team. Every single person on the team has access to these. And whoever is the first person to jump in will flag it. And sometimes you'll see on a Twitter, someone will write a question, there's three people from Deel team has answered. We're like, "Okay, I think enough of us have provided value here."
turns.zh: 从来不是自动化的。直到今天也不是。我们永远不会把和人们的互动自动化。早期，是我自己、团队里其他人、我们的联合创始人——顺便说一句，他们至今还在做。所以团队里很多人都在做。团队里每个人都有这些渠道的访问权限。谁先跳进去谁就先标记。有时候你会在 Twitter 上看到，有人写了个问题，结果有三个 Deel 团队的人回答了。我们会说，"好吧，我觉得我们提供价值已经够多了。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing. And I'm spending a lot of time on this, but this is such an interesting and important tactic that clearly worked to help you all start and it's cheap. And most, at least B2B, companies could probably leverage this. So when people are thinking about where to go, maybe do this, you mentioned Twitter, maybe Reddit, maybe Quora. Is there anything else, just like the sphere of potential places founders can go think about whether maybe people are asking questions they could answer there?
turns.zh: 这太厉害了。我在这上面花了好多时间，但这真的是一个既有趣又重要的战术，它显然帮你们起步了，而且成本很低。而且至少大多数 B2B 公司大概都能利用这个。所以当人们在想该去哪里、也许该这么做时，你提到了 Twitter、Reddit、Quora。还有别的吗，就是创始人可以去考虑的、潜在地方的范围——看那里有没有人在问他们能回答的问题？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yeah, there are a lot of closed communities, so there are still ... they could be Slack communities, Discord, places that founders choose to connect with other founders. Or we have partnerships with places like the Y Combinator, where once you go through a certain program or you qualify to be in the club, whatever that club may be, you get to get access to this community where you can talk to other people. So those are considered closed communities. It's not as easy to gain access to. But if you can find a way to gain access to those communities, they're also great places to be.
turns.zh: 是的，有很多封闭社区，所以还有……可能是 Slack 社区、Discord，创始人选择和其他创始人联系的地方。或者我们和像 Y Combinator 这样的地方有合作，一旦你通过了某个项目或者你有资格进入那个俱乐部（不管那个俱乐部是什么），你就能获得这个社区的访问权，可以和其他人交谈。所以那些算是封闭社区。不那么容易进入。但如果你能找到进入这些社区的方法，它们也是很棒的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then step number one is add value, right?
turns.zh: 然后第一步就是增加价值，对吧？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You can't just get in the community, "Hey, check out Deel everyone."
turns.zh: 你不能只是进到社区里说，"嘿，大家来看看 Deel。"

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Otherwise you'll just get kicked out. You can try not adding value, you're not going to last very long.
turns.zh: 否则你只会被踢出去。你可以试着不增加价值，但你待不了多久。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. If you think about the pie chart of how growth happened at Deel early on and then today, what would that roughly look like? What percentage of early growth came through this versus SEO or whatever else worked, and then today? Whatever you can share of where growth comes from.
turns.zh: 对。如果你想想 Deel 早期和今天增长是怎么发生的饼图，那大概会是什么样子？早期增长有多少来自这个，对比 SEO 或其他有效手段，然后今天呢？你能分享的关于增长来源的任何信息。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Today, roughly about I would say 50% of our growth continues to come from what we would consider non-paid channels, through whether it be partnerships, SEO, these kinds of moderations. So early on that was more close to 80% to 90%. But that number has grown. Again, the net number has grown, but the percentage of the overall value has shrunk because other channels have also grown significantly.
turns.zh: 今天，我会说大约 50% 的增长继续来自我们认为是非付费渠道的地方，无论是通过合作、SEO，还是这类"审核/引导"工作。所以早期这个数字更接近 80% 到 90%。但那个数字增长了。再说一次，净数字增长了，但占总价值的百分比缩小了，因为其他渠道也显著增长了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So let's talk about SEO. First of all, how important has that been to the success and growth of Deel? And then also just what have you learned about what is important to get SEO right?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好，那我们聊聊 SEO。首先，它对 Deel 的成功和增长有多重要？还有，你学到了什么关于把 SEO 做对的关键点？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yeah. So I would say for SEO, the biggest mistake people make is they will just shove keywords. They're like, "Okay, these are the keywords people are searching for, I need to make sure I mention it five times." Obviously do that, make sure that the content that you wrote answers the question. But the main thing to think about it is, is the Google search over? If someone reads your content, if they typed in something to Google, and then they read the article that you've published, are they going back to Google to continue reading more or is the Google search over? Because ultimately that's what the search engines care about is, I want to make sure this person gets their answer quickest way possible.
turns.zh: 是的。所以对于 SEO，人们犯的最大错误就是硬塞关键词。他们想，"好，这些是人们在搜的关键词，我得确保提它五遍。"显然要做这个，确保你写的内容回答了那个问题。但主要的思考角度是：Google 搜索结束了吗？如果有人读了你的内容，如果他们往 Google 里输入了什么，然后读了你发布的文章，他们是要回到 Google 继续读更多，还是 Google 搜索就到此结束了？因为说到底，搜索引擎关心的是：我想确保这个人以最快的方式得到他的答案。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So when you think from that perspective, it's much easier to actually write things that people want to read, and you're not just meandering and going on and on, shoving a bunch of keywords that people are just like, "I'm bored, I'm bouncing, I'm going somewhere else."
turns.zh: 所以当你从那个角度思考，就更容易写出人们想读的东西，你不会只是在那儿漫无目的地啰嗦，塞一堆关键词让人们想"好无聊，我要跳走了，去别的地方"。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So asking that question of, is the search over is a really good place to start, instead of just shoving keywords. And our content team is amazing. I would say they're more of an operational team than they are a creative team. The way they run things, the way they publish the articles, there's a very clear framework that is used to decide what gets published when and what doesn't get published by the same token. So all of those things are very important to consider, instead of just being like, "Oh, this keyword has 10,000 monthly visitors, I'm just going to write a bunch of things about that."
turns.zh: 所以问"搜索结束了吗"这个问题，是一个非常不错的起点，而不是只塞关键词。而且我们的内容团队非常棒。我会说他们更像一个运营团队，而不是一个创意团队。他们运作的方式、发布文章的方式，都有一个非常清晰的框架，来决定什么该在什么时候发布、什么不该发布。所以所有这些事情都很重要，要去考虑，而不是只想着"哦，这个关键词每月有一万访客，我就写一堆关于它的东西"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's an example of a page that you wrote that ends people search and gives them what they need?
turns.zh: 有没有一个你写的、能终结人们搜索并给他们所需东西的页面的例子？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: A lot of people wonder what an EOR is because that's an employer of record. They tend to be confused about exactly what that is. So we do very well in explaining to people what EOR is and isn't and what its limitations are. Because the first question that you will have after the EOR question's answered is, okay, what's the downside? When do I need to not use it? So for us, that's one of the content pieces that does very well.
turns.zh: 很多人想知道什么是 EOR，因为那是 Employer of Record（雇主记录）。他们往往搞不清那到底是什么。所以我们很擅长向人们解释 EOR 是什么、不是什么，以及它的局限性。因为你在这个 EOR 问题被回答后，第一个问题会是：好，缺点是什么？我什么时候不该用它？所以对我们来说，这是表现很好的内容之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd love to spend more time on this operational element of the SEO team. Maybe one question is just what is that bar that tells you that it's ready to publish and worth going out versus it's not ready?
turns.zh: 我想多花点时间在这个 SEO 团队的运营元素上。也许一个问题是：那个告诉你"它准备好发布了、值得推出"和"它还没准备好"的门槛是什么？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yes. So I can't take credit to this, this is all of our team's work. But we have this framework that we call the traffic light system. Essentially we go, whenever the team is going to do a content series, they will go and find up to 700 keywords. These are keywords that are related to what we do. So they might be closely related, they might be distant related. And then those set of keywords get ranked by highest volume to the lowest volume. So then you have an Excel sheet, keywords on the left, volume on the right. And then you go one by one. This does take time. And then say, what is the intent of someone searching this keyword?
turns.zh: 是的。所以这个我没法居功，这全是我们团队的功劳。但我们有一个我们称之为红绿灯系统的框架。本质上，每当团队要做一个内容系列，他们会去找多达 700 个关键词。这些关键词都和我们的业务相关。所以可能是紧密相关的，也可能是关系较远的。然后这组关键词会按搜索量从高到低排序。所以你就有了个 Excel 表，左边是关键词，右边是搜索量。然后你一个一个过。这确实需要时间。然后问，搜索这个关键词的人的意图是什么？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Is this a university student looking to write an article and they're never going to become our customer? Or is this someone that is actually looking to solve their existing solution and they are going to become our customer? So with that, you get the green light ones, which is the intent is very high, this person wants our solution. The yellow light is intent, could be they are a 50:50, maybe they're looking to buy our solution, maybe it's not soon enough. And then the red is, this person is not looking to buy our solution, they're just doing this search for any other reason. So when you do that, then you go from the greens, highest volume to the lowest volume, yellows, highest volume to the lowest volume, and oftentimes you never get to the reds.
turns.zh: 这是一个想写篇文章、永远不会成为我们客户的大学生吗？还是说这是一个真的想解决他现有问题、并且会成为我们客户的人？所以这样你就得到了绿灯类——意图非常高，这个人想要我们的方案。黄灯类是意图，可能是 50:50，也许他们想买我们的方案，也许还不那么快。然后红灯类是，这个人不是在找我们的方案，他们只是因为任何其他原因做这个搜索。所以当你这么做时，你就从绿灯、搜索量从高到低开始，然后黄灯、搜索量从高到低，而红灯常常根本轮不到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. And then once you have say a keyword, say a green, I guess, it's a green keyword where it's high intent and high volume, what is the process to actually put together an article that works for SEO?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。然后一旦你有一个比如绿灯的关键词——我猜就是高意图、高搜索量的——实际去拼出一篇对 SEO 有效的文章，流程是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So step one is understanding the search intent. Why is someone typing that? What are they trying to understand? And a part of that is going to Google and figuring out, what is Google servicing today? So one of the examples that I always give people of when you type EOR into Google, it doesn't give you employer of record, it gives you enhanced oil recovery, because most of the people typing EOR to Google is looking for that solution.
turns.zh: 所以第一步是理解搜索意图。为什么有人打这个词？他们想弄明白什么？这部分要去 Google 弄清楚：Google 今天在提供什么？所以我常给人们举的一个例子是，当你在 Google 里打 EOR，它给出的不是 employer of record，而是 enhanced oil recovery（强化采油），因为大多数往 Google 打 EOR 的人是在找那个方案。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Now, if my team blindly went in and said, "We're going to rank for EOR," we're never going to rank for that because that's not what Google gives people because that's not what people have been looking for. So first is understanding, what are people looking for? And creating a content piece that answers those questions. Oftentimes the bottom part of Google where it says, the next questions that you should be asking is a really good place to go to understand, okay, after someone's done with this search, what's the next question that they ask? And the next one and the next one.
turns.zh: 现在，如果我的团队盲目地进去说"我们要为 EOR 排名"，我们永远排不上去，因为那不是 Google 给人们的东西，因为那不是人们在找的。所以首先是理解：人们在找什么？然后创作一个回答那些问题的内容。很多时候 Google 底部的"人们还问"——也就是你接下来应该问的问题——是一个很好的去处，用来理解：某人在做完这个搜索后，他下一个问的是什么？然后一个接一个。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So figuring out what do people want to get out of this? And then there are a myriad of SEO solutions tools that you can use out there to ensure that the content you've written is in a simple enough language that someone with a fifth grade reading level can understand. That you actually did the right things, you put the right keywords in the right places. I almost think of keywords as like, that's your address, that's how you give Google, please send people my way. So you can use many tools.
turns.zh: 所以弄清楚人们想从这里面得到什么。然后有各种各样你可以用的 SEO 解决方案工具，来确保你写的内容语言足够简单，一个五年级阅读水平的人都能理解。确保你做对了那些事，把正确的关键词放在正确的位置。我几乎把关键词看作——那是你的地址，那是你告诉 Google"请把人往我这边送"的方式。所以你可以用很多工具。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: We use Clearscope, we love it. So those are the tools that you use. And then it gets published. And oftentimes those tools will give you a score to say you're an A plus or you're a C minus, you need to make your language less sophisticated, currently it's at university level and we need it to be at fourth grade reading level.
turns.zh: 我们用 Clearscope，我们很喜欢它。所以那些就是你用的工具。然后就发布了。而且那些工具经常会给你一个分数，说你是 A+ 还是 C-，你需要让语言不那么复杂，目前它在大学水平，我们需要它到四年级阅读水平。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is the structure of the content team at this point, how many people is it, and what are their rough focuses?
turns.zh: 这个内容团队现在的结构是什么，大概多少人，他们各自的侧重点是什么？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Fun fact about our content team, the person that leads it was one of the earliest employees at Deel, I want to say number two or three. So the person there is just so special to our entire company. And so the structure of the content team for us is, it is led by our director of content. We have one person that is in charge of all of the operations. So that is working with our freelancers, making sure that the briefs are sent out, making sure that the fact checking is done on time, that the articles are published on the website, and tracking and everything, they run the machinery on the backend.
turns.zh: 关于我们内容团队一个有趣的事实是，领导它的人是 Deel 最早的员工之一，我想说是第二或第三号。所以那个人对我们整个公司来说非常特别。所以对我们来说内容团队的结构是：由我们的内容总监领导。我们有一个人负责所有运营。也就是和我们的自由撰稿人合作、确保 brief 发出去、确保事实核查按时完成、文章在网站上发布，以及追踪等等，他们在后台运转这台机器。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And then we have different people focused on different areas of content because you need to have expertise that you build over time to write properly. So we have one person looking after certain product lines, another person would be focusing on [inaudible 00:22:46] behind different product lines. And very recently we've set out a team for different types of content because content isn't just written article, it's also video, it's also education. There's a lot of different types of content that we want to tap into. So now there's a team that is focused on those new mediums for us.
turns.zh: 然后我们有不同的人专注于不同领域的内容，因为你需要有随着时间建立的专长才能写好。所以我们有一个人看某些产品线，另一个人专注于不同产品线背后的[inaudible 00:22:46]。而且最近我们为不同类型的内容组建了一个团队，因为内容不只是写的文章，它也是视频，也是教育。有很多不同类型的内容我们想切入。所以现在有一个团队专注于那些对我们来说的新媒介。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So how many people total full-time that run this operation?
turns.zh: 太棒了。那运行这个运营的全职人员总共有多少？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Right now the team is about eight people total.
turns.zh: 现在团队总共大概八个人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's like, I don't know if it's exactly 50% of it, something like half of your growth essentially is coming from this team?
turns.zh: 而且，我不知道是不是正好 50%，但大致上你一半的增长其实是来自这个团队？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else you found that it's really important or effective for thinking about making SEO work?
turns.zh: 有没有什么是你发现对于思考如何让 SEO 真正起作用，非常重要或有效的？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: The biggest mistake people make is SEO is one of those things that, you can try and automate it, you can do a lot of things that save you time, but it never stops being time-consuming. And to do it well, it is going to be time-consuming. So oftentimes people just get over it or they think it's below them to be going over and doing keyword research and doing all of those things one by one. And that's oftentimes where people lose out is they try to cut corners. And when you cut corners, you just don't create a good quality resource. That's what it comes down to. It's like, is your resource good quality? Yes or no?
turns.zh: 人们犯的最大错误之一是，SEO 是那种你试图去自动化、你可以做很多省时间的事情，但它永远不会不再耗费时间。要把它做好，它必然会耗费时间。所以人们经常就放弃了，或者觉得做关键词研究、一个一个做那些事情是低于自己身份的事。而这往往就是人们输掉的地方——他们试图走捷径。而当你走捷径时，你就是没能创造出一个高质量的资源。说到底就是：你的资源质量高吗？是或否？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So when you try to just be like, I want to rank and cut all those corners, your content is not going to be great. Nobody's going to want to read it. And your program is not going to go anywhere. So I think it's one of those things that people as they become more senior think it's below them. And I think that's the biggest mistake.
turns.zh: 所以当你只是想"我要排名，然后把所有那些捷径都抄了"，你的内容就不会好。没人会想读它。你的项目也走不远。所以我觉得这是那种事情之一：人们越资深，就越觉得这低于自己身份。我觉得这是最大的错误。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting, and that's exactly the same advice for writing a newsletter, the thing I do. Where if a newsletter isn't working, it usually means the content isn't valuable enough to people. It's such a clear meritocracy of, if it's useful, people will read it, subscribe, share. And if they're not, they won't subscribe. And then Google basically figures that out based on people's behavior.
turns.zh: 这很有意思，而且这和我做的一件事——写通讯——的建议完全一样。如果一份通讯不起作用，通常意味着内容对人们来说不够有价值。这是一个非常清晰的优胜劣汰：如果有用，人们就会读、订阅、分享。如果没有，他们就不会订阅。然后 Google 基本上会根据人们的行为搞清楚这一点。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yes, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To give people a sense of the operation, how many articles are you putting out a month, a day, a week, whatever you can share there?
turns.zh: 为了让人们对这个运营有个概念，你们一个月、一天、一周发布多少篇文章，任何你能分享的数字？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: We used to put out about 10 articles a week, that's net new. Whereas now we are doing more of five new articles and five article updates. Because the type of content we write, regulations change, things change all the time, so we need to make sure that even if something was published two years ago, it's up-to-date. So we have a team that is responsible for continuously fact checking. So we do about five article updates and five net new articles written. And of course we do it across many different languages. So what started off as English only operations is now in other languages as well. So there's no shortage of work to go around.
turns.zh: 我们以前大概一周发 10 篇文章，是全新的。而现在我们在做的是大约 5 篇新文章加 5 篇文章更新。因为我们写的内容类型，法规会变，事情一直在变，所以我们需要确保即使某篇是两年前发布的，它也是最新的。所以我们有一个团队负责持续的事实核查。所以我们做大约 5 篇更新和 5 篇全新文章。当然我们还跨多种语言来做。所以从最初只有英语的运营，现在也覆盖其他语言了。所以活儿一点都不缺。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that I go back and forth on a bit is, if SEO is something every company should be doing and will work for them? And in my experience, there's certain products that are really good for SEO, especially if there's user generated content or there's just a bunch of data like say Yelp or Glassdoor, where they can generate tons of pages in all these different ways. Do you have an opinion on what sort of business and company is best suited for SEO? Or is your feeling everyone should probably be doing SEO in some form? And even if it's not a huge part of your growth strategy, it'll help.
turns.zh: 有件事我有点犹豫不决：SEO 是不是每家公司都应该做、并且对它们都有效？根据我的经验，有些产品特别适合 SEO，尤其是有用户生成内容、或者像 Yelp 或 Glassdoor 那样有一大堆数据、能以各种方式生成大量页面的产品。你对于什么样的业务和公司最适合 SEO 有什么看法？还是说你的感觉是，每个人都应该以某种形式做 SEO？即使它不是你增长战略的一大部分，它也会有帮忙。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: I don't think everybody should be doing SEO. I think if you are in a space where people are looking for a solution, you should be doing SEO. But if you are a direct to consumer company selling people lipstick, which I'm a huge buyer of, you probably shouldn't invest in SEO all that much because people don't go to Google for that. They go to Instagram, they go to influencers. And even if someone types in the best lipstick of 2023, chances of your website ranking, because you're not a third party objective comparing to other people, is very low. So it really depends on the solution. But if you are in a space which most B2B products tend to be, that you're solving an active problem very specifically, then I would say SEO is a good idea. If you're a consumer good, maybe a little bit less effort should be put towards it.
turns.zh: 我不认为每个人都该做 SEO。我觉得如果你所在的领域是人们在找解决方案，你就应该做 SEO。但如果你是一家直接面向消费者的公司，卖人们口红——而我是个大买家——你大概不该在 SEO 上投入太多，因为人们不会去 Google 找这个。他们去 Instagram，去找网红。而且即使有人打了"2023 年最佳口红"，你的网站排上去的概率也非常低，因为你不是和其他人做客观第三方对比的角色。所以这真的取决于解决方案。但如果你所在的领域——大多数 B2B 产品往往都是——你在非常具体地解决一个切实的问题，那我会说 SEO 是个好主意。如果你是消费品，也许应该在它上面少花点精力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makes a lot of sense. Going back to the early days, you were hired as head of growth at Deel, there's a lot of things you could do. I'm curious how you decided where to prioritize your resources and what to do in the early days? Versus what you started doing down the road and what you could almost not worry about early on? What have you learned about that early prioritization exercise?
turns.zh: 很有道理。回到早期，你被聘为 Deel 的增长负责人，有很多事情你可以做。我很好奇你是怎么决定把资源优先级放在哪、早期该做什么的？对比你后来开始做的事情，以及早期你几乎不用去担心的？关于那个早期的优先级排序练习，你学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yes. So I would say early days, it's very important to just go back to the basics, build the skeleton before you put on the makeup. So the first question I would ask is, do you have a website? Is it fast? Do the search engine knows that it exists? Okay, great. The next step would be, can people find it? If they can't find it, you need to write content to make sure that people can find it.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我会说早期阶段，回归基础非常重要——先搭好骨架，再化妆打扮。所以我会先问的第一个问题是：你有网站吗？它快吗？搜索引擎知道它的存在吗？好的，很棒。下一步就是：人们能找到它吗？如果找不到，你需要写内容来确保人们能找到它。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Only after all of those questions are answered, should you then consider, do I have money? Can I put it behind some paid ads to make sure people come to my website? So going step-by-step. But you can't run a successful paid ads program if you have a website that's loading in four plus seconds. So really going back to the basics and starting from a good experience at the core. And then expanding step-by-step from there is how I would suggest everybody starts. And that's what I would do if I was to get hired all over again.
turns.zh: 只有把这些问题都回答完了，你才应该考虑：我有钱吗？我能不能把它放到付费广告后面，来确保人们访问我的网站？所以要一步步来。但如果你的网站加载需要四秒以上，你就没法跑一个成功的付费广告项目。所以真的要回归基础，从一个好的核心体验开始。然后再一步步地从那里扩展，这就是我建议每个人开始的方式。如果我重新被雇佣，我也会这么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. So what are some of the steps? So step one is, do you have a website? Step two is make sure the website performs and people can actually have a good time when they're experiencing it. I imagine part of it is also, do people understand what you do, like tweaking maybe the pitch and the [inaudible 00:28:07]
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。那有哪些步骤？第一步，你有网站吗？第二步，确保网站表现好，人们在体验时真的能有个好时光。我想其中一部分也是，人们理解你是做什么的吗，比如调整一下你的 pitch 和[inaudible 00:28:07]

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yes, exactly. And speaking of the pitch, our copy team does an amazing job at this. In the B2B world, it's very easy to come up with statements that could so easily be applied to another business and it would work just as well on their website. And it sounds good and you and your team feel really good about it. But then if your one-liner can also work for another business, please don't let that be your one-liner. Make it so that people actually understand what you do. Because right now there's a lot of statements out there like, 'we do the complex things so you can focus on what you do best', what does that mean? And you can give that to 90% of the B2B businesses out there and it would apply to them, which means it's not good enough.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。说到 pitch，我们的文案团队在这方面做得非常棒。在 B2B 世界里，很容易写出那些套到另一家公司身上也照样好用、在他们网站上一样成立的陈述。它听起来不错，你和你的团队也感觉很好。但如果你的那句一句话介绍也能用在另一家公司身上，那就别让它成为你的一句话介绍。要让人真正理解你是做什么的。因为现在外面有很多像"我们做复杂的事，让你专注做你最擅长的事"这样的陈述——这到底是什么意思？你把它给外面 90% 的 B2B 公司，它都适用，那就意味着它不够好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything that you remember you changed in those early days in terms of the website or the positioning or anything along those lines that was a big improvement?
turns.zh: 在早期那些日子里，在网站、定位或任何类似方面，你记得你做了什么改动，带来了很大的改善吗？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Our website was hard coded, so the first thing we did with the help of the dev team was to move it to a platform that it was easy for me to access and edit, so that we could continuously A/B test things. And outside of that, we worked really hard on testing a lot of value propositions to explain to people exactly what we do, explain problem first, solution first, and time savings, cost savings, putting a lot of those against each other and rapidly A/B testing.
turns.zh: 我们的网站是硬编码的，所以我们在开发团队帮助下做的第一件事，就是把它迁移到一个我能轻松访问和编辑的平台上，这样我们就能持续做 A/B 测试。除此之外，我们非常努力地测试了很多价值主张，来向人们精确解释我们是做什么的，先解释问题、先解释方案，以及时间节省、成本节省，把很多这些东西互相做对比，并快速做 A/B 测试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Once you got past that phase, where maybe you started doing some paid ads and other things, where did you find you could invest more resources?
turns.zh: 一旦你度过了那个阶段——也许你开始做一些付费广告和其他事情了——你发现你可以投入更多资源的地方在哪里？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Once we covered the basics of your big four or five ad platforms, we started looking into the long tail places. So those are the platforms that individually never contribute a significant enough chunk for you to individually care about it. But if you add them up, it diversifies your lead flow such that it ends up being about 30% of your overall lead flow that's coming in. Those could be things like review sites or much smaller outlets that could also run ads, newsletter ads, podcast ads, all of those things.
turns.zh: 一旦我们覆盖了你那四五个大广告平台的基础，我们就开始看长尾的地方。也就是那些单独看永远贡献不了足够大一块、让你单独去在意它的平台。但如果你把它们加起来，它就让你的线索来源多样化了，最终占到你整体线索流的约 30%。这些可能是评论网站、或者小得多的也能跑广告的渠道、通讯广告、播客广告，所有这些东西。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: When you run an individual podcast ad, yeah, you're probably not going to get 2000 customers from one podcast. But you run 10 of those and then it starts adding up. So really long tail is where we focused on. And we started going very niche with websites that have maybe 50,000, a hundred thousand visitors a month, which isn't all that much when you're thinking about your paid ad strategy. But all of those places add up and they're oftentimes overlooked because they're not as easy, you have to take the time to set up from scratch to run it on everything. Our paid ads team, they spent just as much time running Facebook and Google ads as they do running those third party, much smaller platform ads. It takes the same effort, but you need to have a diversified source of your leads.
turns.zh: 当你跑一个单独的播客广告时，是的，你大概不会从一个播客获得 2000 个客户。但你跑 10 个这样的，它就开始累积了。所以真正的长尾才是我们关注的地方。我们开始非常垂直地去做那些每月可能有 5 万、10 万访客的网站，这在你考虑付费广告战略时并不算多。但所有这些地方加起来，而且它们经常被人忽视，因为它们不那么容易，你得花时间从零开始在每个上面设置来跑。我们的付费广告团队，花在跑 Facebook 和 Google 广告上的时间和跑那些第三方、小得多的平台广告上一样多。它花费同样的精力，但你需要有一个多样化的线索来源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Huge fan of podcast ads over here, and maybe this would be a good time to cue the mid-roll ad, maybe, I don't know, it happens.
turns.zh: 我是播客广告的超级粉丝，也许现在是插播中段广告的好时机，也许，我不知道，它就这么发生了。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Sounds perfect.
turns.zh: 听起来完美。
