turns.en: And welcome back. Speaking of podcast ads, something that I find is with that sort of advertising, there's a direct response component of like, we will drive leads as running an ad like this, and there's also a awareness, brand building component. I know you're not a big fan of awareness campaigns and marketing campaigns, especially early on, and so I'd love to get your perspective on why that is and how you think about that sort of investment?
turns.zh: 欢迎回来。说到播客广告，我发现这类广告有一个直接响应的部分，比如我们跑这样一个广告会带来线索，同时也有一个认知、品牌建设的成分。我知道你不是很喜欢认知营销活动和品牌营销活动，尤其是早期，所以我很想听听你为什么这么看，以及你是怎么看待这类投资的？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: I'm not a huge fan of early awareness campaigns for B2B businesses specifically. So if you are a consumer goods founder, you can skip this part. But the reason I don't like awareness early on is because to do a proper awareness campaign, it takes time. You need to have teams that are doing the strategy, doing the creative work, and they don't always hit. You don't know if they're always going to resonate or not. And then you look back, and you've worked on this thing for a whole month and it hasn't resonated and you've wasted a full month.
turns.zh: 我特别不喜欢早期做认知活动，尤其是针对 B2B 业务。所以如果你是个消费品创始人，这部分可以跳过。但我不喜欢早期做认知的原因是，要做一次恰当的认知活动，需要时间。你需要有团队做战略、做创意工作，而且它们不总是能命中。你不知道它们会不会一直引起共鸣。然后你回头一看，你在这个东西上忙活了整整一个月，它却没引起共鸣，你白白浪费了一个月。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Because B2B businesses uniquely are started because there's a very real need and there's a lot of people that are ready to convert, first tap into the bottom of the funnel, and then go out and start speaking to the masses. But I promise you it'll probably take you six to eight months minimum to tap into that bottom of the funnel of people that are ready to convert today before you have to start doing awareness ads out there. That's not to say never do awareness ads, but it's oftentimes the shiny, cool thing that you want to do and it just ends up being a waste of time early on. Because people don't really even understand what you're doing, you haven't really even figured out what's the messaging that resonates, but you've done this creative campaign and people are like, "This looks cool, but I'm just going to go ahead and continue looking for a solution for my problem."
turns.zh: 因为 B2B 业务独特的地方在于，它们是因为一个非常真实的需求而成立的，而且有很多人已经准备好转化了，所以先切入漏斗底部，然后再出去开始对大众说话。但我向你保证，在你不得不开始做外面的认知广告之前，大概至少要花六到八个月去切入那些今天准备好转化的漏斗底部人群。这并不是说永远别做认知广告，但它往往是那个你想做的、闪亮又酷的东西，结果在早期就是浪费时间。因为人们甚至还不理解你在做什么，你甚至还没搞清楚什么信息能引起共鸣，但你已经做了这个创意活动，人们就会想，"这看起来很酷，但我就继续去找我问题的解决方案吧。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of a marketing campaign or an awareness campaign that comes to mind that you thought was like, "Okay, this is ... if you do it this way, maybe it's worth doing"?
turns.zh: 有没有一个营销活动或认知活动的例子浮现在你脑海里，让你觉得，"好吧，这个……如果你这样做，也许值得做"？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: I've seen Notion do a great job with their out-of-home ads. They didn't do it early on, they started doing it much later in their journey by the time when everybody that was working in tech knew what it was, and it was really to drive home the message continuously rather than to introduce themselves to the world. So by then when you saw that layout on a billboard, it made sense, you're like, "Oh, I know what they're talking about."
turns.zh: 我见过 Notion 在他们的户外广告上做得很好。他们不是早期做的，而是在旅程晚期才开始做，那时每个在科技行业工作的人都知道它是什么，而它真的是为了持续地把信息钉进人们脑子里，而不是为了向全世界介绍自己。所以到那时，当你在广告牌上看到那个版面，它就有意义了，你会想，"哦，我知道他们在说什么。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what is it about Notion that you think was great, it was timing and then also the actual ad itself you thought was great?
turns.zh: 那么关于 Notion，你觉得很棒的是什么——是时机，还是广告本身你觉得很棒？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yeah, the ads that I'm recalling right now were showcasing their product interface. So they needed enough time, and this is my obviously hypothesis, if someone from Notion wants to jump in and say that wasn't the reason why we did this, go ahead, but I think they needed enough time for people to get familiar with the interface. Because Notion has a very specific interface that when you see it, you recognize it, it's not like any other product. So unless people built that awareness and recognition, doing an out-of-home ad with that layout wouldn't have made much sense because just with that layout they were able to communicate what product they're talking about. If they did that day one, people would be like, "What is this thing that I'm looking at?"
turns.zh: 是的，我现在回忆起的那些广告是在展示他们的产品界面。所以他们需要有足够的时间——这当然只是我的假设，如果 Notion 有人想跳出来说"我们这么做不是因为这个原因"，请便——但我觉得他们需要足够的时间让人们熟悉那个界面。因为 Notion 有一个非常特定的界面，当你看到它你就认得，它不像其他任何产品。所以除非人们建立了那种认知和识别，否则用那个版面做一个户外广告没什么意义，因为他们仅凭那个版面就能传达他们在说哪个产品。如果他们第一天就那么做，人们会想，"我看着的这个东西到底是什么？"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So we've been working through all the ways that Deel has grown, we've talked about SEO, community, you mentioned partnerships. Is there anything interesting there to mention around just what partnerships have done?
turns.zh: 我们已经把 Deel 增长的各种方式都过了一遍，聊了 SEO、社区，你提到了合作。在合作方面，有没有什么有趣的值得一提的，就是合作都做了些什么？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yeah, I would say it is very important to know who you should partner with. So there's two groups of partners. People oftentimes end up partnering with any company that has a shared audience. Decent place to start. But just because you share an audience doesn't mean your audience goes to your partner for guidance when they have this problem.
turns.zh: 是的，我会说知道该和谁合作非常重要。所以合作伙伴有两类。人们经常最终和任何有共同受众的公司合作。这是个不错的起点。但仅仅因为你们共享一个受众，并不意味着你的受众在遇到这个问题时会去找你的合作伙伴寻求指导。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So in our case, venture capital partners was a huge one because when you get money from a new VC, they ask, they're like, "Okay, thank you for giving us this money, now we want to expand our team with the money you gave us. What are your other portfolio companies using? What is a platform that you trust that you would recommend?" So people go to their VCs for that kind of question. But there might be another tech company out there that is tapping into the exact audience that we are, but people never go to them to ask that question. So our partnership with them will likely not work just as well. So it's important to not only recognize the importance of an audience overlap as well as whether or not those people are seen as a trusted resource for the solution you are putting out there.
turns.zh: 所以在我们的情况里，风险投资合作伙伴是一个巨大的类别，因为当你从一家新 VC 拿到钱时，他们会问，他们会说，"好，谢谢你给我们这笔钱，现在我们用你给的钱来扩展我们的团队。你的其他投资组合公司在用什么？你信任、会推荐哪个平台？"所以人们会去找他们的 VC 问这类问题。但外面可能有另一家科技公司，它切入的正是和我们完全相同的受众，但人们从不去他们那里问那个问题。所以我们和他们的合作大概就不会那么有效。所以重要的是，不仅要认识到受众重叠的重要性，还要认识到这些人是否被视为你推出的解决方案的可信资源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really love this idea you keep coming back to, which is where are people asking this question that you can help them answer. And to make that even more concrete for people, what are some other examples maybe of questions people ask that Deel can help them with? So that it could help people think about, okay, maybe our product can help them answer these other sorts of questions
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢你一直反复提到的这个想法，就是人们都在哪里问这个你能帮他们回答的问题。为了让它对人更具体，有没有其他一些例子，是人们会问、而 Deel 能帮忙回答的问题？这样能帮人们思考，好吧，也许我们的产品能帮他们回答其他这类问题。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Since the early days, and it continues to happen, compliance is a huge question that gets asked. So when you are an HR leader or a finance leader or a legal leader in a company that works let's say in America, but you want to hire someone in another country, you don't know what you don't know. So it's very important to have people that know what they're talking about in context of your country of origin as well as the country that you're trying to hire from. So compliance has always been a huge part of what we did and what we've always answered for people. That's why we have in-house experts that answer those questions, that constantly provide updates if the answer to that question has changed over time, which regulations constantly change. An answer we provided a week ago may change, and you need to be very proactive in communicating that.
turns.zh: 从早期开始——而且一直在发生——合规是一个被问得非常多的问题。所以当你是一家公司的 HR 负责人、财务负责人或法务负责人，这家公司比如在美国运作，但你想在另一个国家招人，你不知道你不知道的东西。所以非常重要的一点是，要有既懂你来源国语境、又懂你想招聘的那个国家语境的人。所以合规一直是我们做的、以及我们一直为人们回答的很大一部分。这就是为什么我们有内部专家来回答那些问题，并且如果那个问题的答案随着时间变了（法规一直在变），就持续提供更新。我们一周前提供的答案可能会变，你需要非常主动地去沟通这一点。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Taxes is another one, especially in the space that we're in, payroll, hiring. Taxes change from country to country. You need to know when you need to pay what taxes, when you need to not pay them, and what types of work people do. So those are some of the types of questions that get asked.
turns.zh: 税务是另一个，尤其是在我们所在的这个领域——薪酬、招聘。税务因国家而异。你需要知道什么时候该交什么税、什么时候不用交，以及人们做的是什么类型的工作。所以那些就是一些被问到的问题类型。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So for us, they're very nitty-gritty and use case specific. The taxes you need to pay for someone who is an engineer that's a full-time employee might be very different than who is a designer who is a contractor. So those are the kinds of specifics that we get into with people.
turns.zh: 所以对我们来说，它们非常具体、且与用例相关。你为一个全职工程师雇员要交的税，可能和一个承包商设计师要交的非常不同。所以那些就是我们会和人们深入的具体细节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So it's like, how do I pay taxes for an engineer I'm hiring in Turkey? And then you give them, "Here's the answer," and then it's like, "If you just want us to take care of it for you, then go check out Deel."
turns.zh: 明白了。所以就像是，我怎么为我正在土耳其招的工程师交税？然后你给他们，"这是答案，"然后就像，"如果你就想让我们帮你搞定，那去看看 Deel。"

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Exactly. Rarely the question is what's the best payroll solution? It's like, okay, that's good to make sure what you're leaning towards isn't shit and that other people agree with you. But ultimately it was like you need the best payroll solution because you need to make sure that things aren't going to go wrong.
turns.zh: 没错。很少会有人问"最好的薪酬解决方案是什么？"这种问题，而是像，好吧，确认一下你倾向的那个不是垃圾、而且其他人都同意你就好。但最终它就像你需要最好的薪酬解决方案，因为你需要确保事情不会出错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of answering questions in content, something that you told me is that you wrote a blog post that the IRS ended up linking to as the definitive answer to a question. And I don't think this was at Deel, but can you share that story?
turns.zh: 说到在内容里回答问题，你告诉过我一件事，就是你写了一篇博客文章，结果 IRS（美国国税局）最终把它作为某个问题的权威答案链接了出去。而且我觉得这不在 Deel，但你能分享一下这个故事吗？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yes, actually it was at my previous role. And the person who wrote that article is today at Deel. So he came over to join us there too. But yes, it was right around when Covid happened and the US government rolled out the PPP program. And there was a lot of questions about, do I qualify? If I qualify, how do I apply for this?
turns.zh: 是的，其实那是在我上一份工作。而写那篇文章的人今天在 Deel。所以他后来也加入我们了。但没错，那大概是在 Covid 发生、美国政府推出 PPP 项目的时候。当时有很多问题，比如我有资格吗？如果有资格，我怎么申请？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And at the time the company that I was working for had a lot of customers that were like, "What do I do? I need to gain access to this, but I don't know what to do." So the team there took the time to truly understand how the system works, whether you qualify, what to do. And created this resource for our own customers because we just wanted to help them. And then it ended up being such a good resource that it was linked from the IRS's website being like, "If you have questions, check out this article," which was a great moment of pride. And it just went to show that when you do your best to answer questions and other people don't have the time to do it, no matter who it is, they're going to send people back your way. And it was at the time, it happened to be a big moment of growth.
turns.zh: 当时我工作的那家公司有很多客户像在说，"我该怎么办？我需要拿到这个，但我不知道该做什么。"所以那边的团队花时间真正弄懂了这个系统是怎么运作的、你有没有资格、该做什么。并且为我们的客户创建了这份资源，因为我们只是想帮他们。然后它最终成了一个如此好的资源，以至于被 IRS 的网站链接了出去，像是说"如果你有问题，看看这篇文章"——那是一个让我们非常自豪的时刻。它也正好说明，当你尽力回答问题、而别人没时间做时，不管对方是谁，他们都会把人送回你这里。而且在当时，它碰巧成了一个增长的大时刻。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: It was a very unfortunate instance, we wish we never had to write that, that it never happened. But yeah, that was the story around IRS linking to the company's resource.
turns.zh: 那是一个非常不幸的情况，我们希望我们永远不必写那个，希望它从未发生。但是的，那就是 IRS 链接到公司资源的故事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's the ultimate sign of the question is answered and you're done with it, the IRS decides to link to it. So you're saying that was actually a big driver of growth, IRS traffic. I'm curious how many people actually go read that?
turns.zh: 那是"问题被回答了、你搞定了"的终极标志——IRS 决定链接到它。所以你是说那实际上是一个增长的大驱动力，IRS 的流量。我很好奇到底有多少人真的去读了那个？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So that was huge for that short duration of a few week time when people were trying to apply for PPP. And then it died out, as did PPP.
turns.zh: 所以对于人们尝试申请 PPP 的那短短几周时间，那是巨大的。然后它就消失了，就像 PPP 一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makes sense. One last question around paid, and then I want to move on to a different topic. Is there anything you've learned about what it takes to be successful at paid growth from your experience at Deel?
turns.zh: 有道理。关于付费，最后一个问题，然后我想转到另一个话题。从你在 Deel 的经验里，关于要做好付费增长需要什么，你学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yeah, so a few things. Our paid team spends a lot of time on both the messaging aspect of things as well as the optimization. So optimization is the technical way in which you set your bids, make sure that you don't go over budget, whether or not you can afford that.
turns.zh: 是的，有几件事。我们的付费团队在信息的层面和优化上都花了很多时间。优化是你设置出价、确保不超预算、你是否负担得起的那个技术性的方式。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And then messaging is making sure that if someone sees your ad, whether it's on Instagram, Twitter, Google, that it makes sense for them. So creative fatigue is a real thing. When you put an ad out there that works for three weeks, people get tired of seeing that, you need to constantly update that. So our paid team is actually updating the ads we put out there on a monthly basis with the exception of a few Google ads, which need to be straight to the point. So staying ahead of creative fatigue. Making sure that your messaging also keeps up with your product, even if the ad is working really well, you need to make sure that as your product has evolved, so has the messaging alongside that.
turns.zh: 然后信息层面是确保，如果有人看到你的广告——无论是在 Instagram、Twitter 还是 Google——它对他们是说得通的。所以创意疲劳是真实存在的。当你放出一个管用了三周的广告，人们看腻了，你需要持续更新它。所以我们付费团队实际上在按月更新我们放出去的广告，除了少数几条需要直奔主题的 Google 广告。所以要走在创意疲劳前面。确保你的信息也跟得上你的产品，即使广告效果很好，你也需要确保随着产品演进，信息也一起演进。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And also recognizing, not just looking at the amount of leads that you generated from a campaign, but how many of them actually became a client, and how much money did you actually make from those clients to understand things around payback. Because oftentimes marketers just tend to think about, "Oh, this is a great lead channel and I get so many leads from it." But then you ask that question to sales teams and they're like, "Yeah, I'm busy, but none of these are converting." So it's really important to look at not just the volume that you bring in, but what is the journey of that volume with your business one year out. How much money do you actually make from them to be able to properly decide how much can I spend to win this customer?
turns.zh: 而且还要认识到，不只是看一个活动生成了多少线索，而是其中有多少人真的成了客户、你从这些客户身上实际赚了多少钱，来理解回收期相关的东西。因为营销人员经常倾向于想，"哦，这是个很棒的线索渠道，我从它那得到好多线索。"但然后你问销售团队这个问题，他们会说，"是的，我很忙，但这些一个都没转化。"所以非常重要的是，不只看你带来的量，还要看那个量在你的业务里一年后走到了哪里。你从他们身上实际赚了多少钱，才能正确决定我能花多少钱去赢得这个客户？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And the way that we've done it is we've worked with our data team to set up a dashboard that tracks that in real time. We know an average customer that comes from a Facebook ad, at what rate do they converge from a lead to a qualified opportunity to a closed on.? And then on average, how much money do we make from that customer one year out. So that we can decide, is this a worthy channel for us, do we not want to invest there or are we reaching that peak and we can't continue to invest there.
turns.zh: 我们做这件事的方式是，我们和我们的数据团队一起搭建了一个实时追踪这些的仪表盘。我们知道一个来自 Facebook 广告的平均客户，从线索到合格商机再到成交的转化率是多少。然后平均来说，一年后我们从那个客户身上赚多少钱。这样我们就能决定，这对我们来说是不是一个值得的渠道，我们要不要在那里投资，还是说我们到达了峰值、无法继续在那里投资了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that I should mention as we talk through this is we're talking about all these ways to grow the product, but at the core is a great product that people actually find valuable and want to keep using. And maybe a question there is just how that plays into this whole growth strategy, actually making the product something people want versus all these acquisition channels?
turns.zh: 在我们聊这些的时候我应该提一件事：我们在聊所有这些增长产品的方式，但核心是一个人们真的觉得有价值、并想持续使用的好产品。也许那里的一个问题就是，这整个增长战略里，把产品做成人们想要的东西、对比所有这些获取渠道，是怎么起作用的？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Acquisition channels just straight up don't work if you have a product that doesn't live up to the expectation. I think I personally have been very spoiled and lucky because from the day I joined Deel, the product was top-notch. As I was joining an early stage company, I joined right after series A, I was expecting certain things to be duct taped in the back, it happens. And I was like, "Oh no, the engineers and the product team are, if they say a product can do something, it can do that and more."
turns.zh: 如果你的产品配不上那个期望，获取渠道就完全不起作用。我觉得我个人非常被宠坏、也很幸运，因为从我加入 Deel 那天起，产品就是一流的。当我加入一家早期公司时，我是在 A 轮之后不久加入的，我预期某些东西在背后是用胶带凑合的，这很正常。而我会想，"哦不，工程师和产品团队，如果他们说一个产品能做某件事，它就能做那件事，甚至更多。"

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So early days of my team pitching Deel was people were like, "I don't think you guys can do all of that. I don't believe you." And it was almost like we had to tamper down our messaging so that people would believe us. But you can be the best marketer in the world, if when people come to your product, even if your sales team does a good job at convincing them to become a customer, because you can do that, if the product doesn't live up to the expectations, especially in the B2B world where people aren't going to put up with crappy products, they're going to leave. That's going to get out and people are going to know it's not a worthy product. So that really sits at the core of everything that we do.
turns.zh: 所以早期我的团队去推销 Deel 时，人们会像，"我觉得你们不可能做得了所有那些。我不信你。"而我们几乎得把我们的信息降调，好让人们相信我们。但你可以是这个世界上最好的营销人员，如果人们来到你的产品，即使你的销售团队很好地说服他们成为了客户——因为你能做到——如果产品配不上期望，尤其是在 B2B 世界里，人们不会容忍糟糕的产品，他们会离开。那会传出去，人们会知道它不是个值得的产品。所以那真的是我们做任何事的核心。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: I think it's very easy to take it for granted when you're at a company that has an awesome product, you're like, "It is like this all the time." But one of the things I would encourage anybody looking to join a young company is, ask them what their team breakdown looks like. When I joined Deel, most of the team was product and engineers. So that told me that the core of this business was going to be solid. And then we built out those supporting things like marketing, like sales, like data to surround the product. But if you are talking to an early stage company that's a B2B product and they have six salespeople and two engineers, their product probably isn't going to be great for that much longer.
turns.zh: 我觉得当你在一家有好产品的公司时，很容易想当然，你会想"它一直都是这样的。"但我会鼓励任何想加入年轻公司的人问一件事：问问他们的团队构成是什么样的。当我加入 Deel 时，团队大部分是产品和工程师。所以那告诉我这个业务的核心会是扎实的。然后我们才围绕产品建起那些支撑性的东西，比如营销、销售、数据。但如果你在和一家早期的 B2B 产品公司交谈，而他们有六个销售、两个工程师，他们的产品可能撑不了多久了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Especially if it's an outsourced dev shop doing the product, they're like, "Oh, they'll take care of the product, we'll just sell it." Something else that I think is important to talk about is Covid was an important element of your growth. And so I guess, one, is that true? And then two, just what did you lean into and lean out of in terms of growth during Covid to help people discover Deel when they needed it most, which is basically people going remote in a lot of ways in a lot of companies?
turns.zh: 尤其是如果是一个外包开发公司在做产品，他们会想，"哦，他们会搞定产品的，我们只要卖就行。"另一件我觉得重要、值得聊的事是，Covid 是你增长的一个重要元素。所以我想，第一，这是真的吗？第二，就增长而言，在 Covid 期间你倾向什么、又远离了什么，来在人们最需要它的时候——基本上就是很多公司在很多方面转向远程——帮人们发现 Deel？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So Covid, actually a lot of people think Deel was started as a response to the pandemic, we actually got started before the pandemic and then the pandemic happened. So as sad as it was, it did force people into a pilot program of the vision that we had for the world. It forced people to work remotely, whether that means you're working remotely from someone who lives a block away from you or you are working remotely from someone in Germany. So we did benefit from the fact that everybody was at least forced to test out this hypothesis of, does it work to not be in the same room as the people that you're working with?
turns.zh: 所以 Covid，其实很多人以为 Deel 是作为对疫情的反应而成立的，我们实际上是在疫情之前成立的，然后疫情发生了。所以尽管很悲哀，它确实把人们推进了我们所设想的世界愿景的一个试点项目里。它迫使人们远程工作，无论那意味着你和住在离你一个街区远的人远程工作，还是你和德国的人远程工作。所以我们确实受益于这样一个事实：每个人都至少被迫去测试了这个假设——不和一起工作的人在同一个房间里，能行得通吗？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And one of the questions that we were getting early on as the Covid was coming to an end was, "Are you worried, Covid is coming to an end, that people aren't going to use Deel anymore?" And our response to that has always been, we are not a remote work platform, we're a global work platform. So a lot of these businesses have gone back into offices. We have a lot of customers that asked people to go back to their offices, but now they have offices in Germany and in Canada and in the US and in France. So we were never a remote work company, we were just a global work company.
turns.zh: 在 Covid 接近尾声时，我们早期被问到的一个问题是，"你担不担心，Covid 要结束了，人们就不再用 Deel 了？"而我们对此的回应一直都是：我们不是一个远程工作平台，我们是一个全球工作平台。所以很多这些企业已经回到了办公室。我们有很多客户要求人们回到办公室，但他们现在在德国、加拿大、美国、法国有办公室。所以我们从来不是一家远程工作公司，我们一直是一家全球工作公司。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And remote work, because there was a lot of news coverage happening around it, we just became synonymous with that. So I do think early on we did benefit from being able to provide that solution. And a lot of people saw the reality of like, "Hey, I work just as well with this person as I did when I was in an office with them. Well, the best person that I'm looking for, the job may not be within my region, so let me go ahead and hire them regardless of where they are." People got comfortable with that and more and more companies started moving in that direction.
turns.zh: 而远程工作，因为当时有大量关于它的新闻报道，我们只是变得和它同义了。所以我确实觉得早期我们受益于能够提供那个解决方案。而且很多人看到了现实，像"嘿，我和这个人一起工作，和我以前在办公室和他一起工作一样好。好吧，我要找的最好的那个人，工作可能不在我的地区，所以不管他在哪，我都去雇他。"人们对这个变得舒服了，越来越多的公司开始朝那个方向走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is there anything that ended up being really important in terms of helping Deel grow through that? Like a channel that's just like, "Let's go big on this channel because it seems to be working really well"? Or is it just word of mouth basically and people are just like, "Oh shit, I really need to solve this problem, my hair's on fire, what's out there? Let me go find an answer"?
turns.zh: 有没有什么是最终在帮助 Deel 度过那个时期增长中变得非常重要的？比如一个渠道，就像"让我们在这个渠道上大干一场，因为它似乎真的很好用"？还是说基本上就是口碑，人们就像"哦糟了，我真的需要解决这个问题，我火烧眉毛了，外面有什么？让我去找个答案"？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: I wouldn't say it was word of mouth, maybe very, very early on it was word of mouth, but within the first few months of our operation that stopped being true. Or at least the word of mouth stopped being a smaller percentage of the way in which people discover us. But it's always that people needed a payroll solution, they needed a way to hire independent contractors overseas, and we just were the answer to that. So we consistently put ourselves in front of them and said, "Hey, if you're trying to do this, or if you're already doing it and you're not doing it legally, we can help you do that legally."
turns.zh: 我不会说是口碑，也许非常非常早期是口碑，但在我们运营的头几个月里那就不成立了。或者至少口碑占人们发现我们的方式的比例变小了。但一直都是：人们需要一个薪酬解决方案，他们需要一种方式来在海外雇佣独立承包商，而我们正好就是那个答案。所以我们持续地把自己摆在他们面前说，"嘿，如果你想做这个，或者你已经在做这个但你做得不合法，我们可以帮你合法地做。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to chat about team building, something that I've heard you're exceptional at. And my first question is, early on when you were building the team, the growth team specifically, at Deel, what skills did you find were most important to look for? And what skills and experiences did you find wasn't as important early on that you could sacrifice and wait until later to get?
turns.zh: 我想聊聊团队建设，我听说你在这方面特别出色。我的第一个问题是，早期你在建设团队、特别是 Deel 的增长团队时，你发现最值得找的技能是什么？有哪些技能和经验你发现早期没那么重要、可以牺牲、等到以后再去获取？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Early on one of the first questions I would ask people is, what are the KPIs that you're willing to commit to? So if someone's only willing to commit to lead numbers, that's not good enough. They need to be able to commit to closed one revenue KPRs to really show that they care about the business's bottom line. So it was those people that were willing to commit to the full funnel.
turns.zh: 早期我会问人们的一个首要问题是，你愿意承诺哪些 KPI？所以如果有人只愿意承诺线索数量，那不够好。他们需要能够承诺成交收入 KPI，来真正表明他们在意业务的底线。所以是那些愿意承诺整个漏斗的人。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And also oftentimes people tend to hire from the big companies that they want to become like because the brand name is appealing. But if you're a team of 35 people, and you're trying to hire the director of whatever from a huge company, you need to ask the question of, when did this person join that huge company? Did they join when the company was already 5,000 people and from day one they had all the resources at their disposal? Or were they actually one of the earlier employees who helped that growth? Because oftentimes the mistake I see people make is they'll hire someone from an amazing company that have accomplished amazing things, but they're not used to operating with 10% of the resources that they had. So they're not willing to get down and do the dirty work.
turns.zh: 而且人们经常倾向于从他们想成为的那种大公司招聘，因为品牌名吸引人。但如果你是一个 35 人的团队，而你试图从一家巨无霸公司招一个什么总监，你需要问的问题是：这个人是什么时候加入那家巨无霸公司的？他们是在公司已经有 5000 人、从第一天起就拥有所有可支配资源时加入的？还是他们其实是更早的员工之一，帮助了那个增长？因为我经常看到人们犯的错误是，他们会从一家成就斐然的神奇公司招人，但他们不习惯只用他们曾有资源的 10% 来运作。所以他们不愿意卷起袖子做那些脏活。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And at Deel we have this concept called 'little hands'. I think it's loosely translated from French, someone can correct me on that. But it basically means that no matter who you are, where you sit within the organization, you need to be willing to get into the little things and do the nitty-gritty work and not shy away from it. And it's very important too, whoever we hire at any level, it's like, "Are you willing to do the tiniest of jobs?" And if the answer is yes, that's great. And some people are like, "I would build a team for that." And of course in the future, maybe you should, but that shouldn't be your first answer. Your first answer should be, "Yes, of course I'll do that." And if someone's not excited about that, then they're not a good fit for at least a company at our stage right now.
turns.zh: 而在 Deel 我们有一个概念叫"little hands"（小手）。我觉得它大概是从法语 loosely 翻译过来的，有人可以纠正我。但它基本上意思是，无论你是谁、你在组织里的什么位置，你都需要愿意钻进那些小事情里、做那些具体的苦活，而不回避它。这也非常重要——无论我们招什么级别的人，都是像"你愿意做最小的工作吗？"如果答案是愿意，那就很棒。而有些人会说"我会为那个建个团队。"当然未来也许你应该，但那不应该是你的第一反应。你的第一反应应该是"是的，我当然会做那个。"如果有人对此不兴奋，那他们至少不适合我们现阶段这样的公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an amazing expression, little hands. You talked about how you check that people are willing to commit to revenue goals. Is that in the interview or is that ... how do you ... because won't everyone just say, "Yeah, yeah, I can commit to anything you need me to commit to, I'm going to go make this work"? How do you get a sense if they're the kind of person that would do that?
turns.zh: 那个表达太妙了，little hands（小手）。你谈到了你怎么核查人们愿意承诺收入目标。那是在面试里还是……你怎么……因为难道大家不会都说"是啊是啊，我可以承诺你需要我承诺的任何东西，我会让它成功"吗？你怎么判断他们是不是那种会这么做的人？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: It happens within the interview process. So one ways to find out is what are the KPIs that they have committed to in the past in their roles. So if they've never committed to a revenue goal or a bottom funnel goal and they're saying they're willing to commit to it, that's probably not correct. And I always say, if they haven't, I say, "What are the KPIs that you have today and what are the KPIs that you think you should have?" Because sometimes they're just not given those, but they still think they should have been given the more bottom funnel. So that's something that I would look for in the interview process.
turns.zh: 它发生在面试过程中。所以一种搞清楚的方式是，他们在过去的角色里承诺过哪些 KPI。所以如果他们从未承诺过收入目标或底部漏斗目标，而他们说愿意承诺，那大概不对。而且我总是说，如果他们没承诺过，我会说"你今天有哪些 KPI、你觉得你该有哪些 KPI？"因为有时候只是没给他们那些，但他们仍然觉得本该给他们更底部漏斗的。所以那是我在面试过程中会找的东西。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And a really good way to also test for that is, this is more on the case study process, but asking someone to come up with a strategy with $0, with $10,000 and maybe a hundred thousand dollars to see if they're going to be able to scale with you. And to see how are they thinking about with different levels of spend and what are they willing to commit to at different levels of spend. Because if someone's throwing up their hands and saying, "At $0, I can only do social media monitoring, we're not going to get much because that's what makes sense." Well, you probably know that they're not going to be comfortable committing to those bottom of funnel metrics until you give them all the resources that they need.
turns.zh: 而且一个很好的测试方式——更多是在案例研究过程里——是让某人用 0 美元、1 万美元、也许 10 万美元来想出一个策略，看他们能不能随着你一起扩展。看他们怎么用不同水平的花费思考，以及在不同花费水平上他们愿意承诺什么。因为如果有人摊开双手说"在 0 美元时，我只能做社媒监控，我们不会得到太多，因为那才说得通"——那你可能知道，在你给他们所需的所有资源之前，他们是不会舒服地承诺那些底部漏斗指标的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it sounds like the way you goal teams within Deel also is revenue, growth teams basically have revenue goals. It's not, like you said, leads or traffic or anything like that.
turns.zh: 听起来你在 Deel 内部给团队定目标的方式也是收入，增长团队基本上有收入目标。不是像你说的，线索或流量或任何这类东西。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yes. That's why we're called growth instead of marketing, we care about the revenue growth. And of course we track leads and SQLs. Those are leading indicators to know whether or not we're going to hit the ultimate number that we all care about. But at the end of the day, that's not what we consider success.
turns.zh: 是的。这就是为什么我们叫增长而不是营销，我们在意的是收入增长。当然我们也追踪线索和 SQL（销售合格线索）。那些是先行指标，用来知道我们能不能达到我们都在意的那个终极数字。但说到底，那不是我们视为成功的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In terms of team structure, how you thought about structuring the early growth team, what did that look like and what was the reporting lines and buckets of investment?
turns.zh: 就团队结构而言，你是怎么思考搭建早期增长团队的，那是什么样子，汇报线和投资的分桶是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yeah, so very early on, we always seek to bring in one leader to manage a part of the organization and then let them grow their teams. We don't love the idea of hiring people based off of a hypothesis that something is going to work. That's a really good way to have to do layoffs because the plans you thought were going to work didn't work. So we always hired one person, prove out a theory, and then let them grow their team.
turns.zh: 是的，所以非常早期，我们总是寻求引入一个负责人来管理组织的一个部分，然后让他们去发展自己的团队。我们不喜欢基于"某个东西会管用"的假设去招人。那是导致不得不做裁员的绝好方式，因为你以为会管用的计划没管用。所以我们总是先招一个人，验证一个理论，然后让他们发展自己的团队。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So the first hire we made to the team was actually a product marketing person. To this day they lead our product marketing team, and they were the ones who sit between the product team and the go-to-market teams and really set the messaging. And quickly we realized this person needs more help in setting the messaging, the tone. So then the second person we hired was a very talented copywriter. And that person today leads our creative teams.
turns.zh: 所以我们给团队招的第一个人其实是一个产品营销的人。直到今天他们领导着我们的产品营销团队，他们是坐在产品团队和进入市场团队之间、真正设定信息的人。然后我们很快意识到这个人在设定信息、语调上需要更多帮助。所以我们招的第二个人是一个非常厉害的文案。而那个人今天领导着我们的创意团队。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And then the third person we actually hired onto the growth team was a data analyst because the sentiment was we're not willing to spend a dollar if we don't know where that money's going and what it's doing for us. Which a lot of people would assume that's a very early hire for ... data is too early to hire as number three. But I still think that we did the right thing there. Now we have a whole data team, but back then we didn't.
turns.zh: 然后我们实际招进增长团队的第三个人是一个数据分析师，因为我们的态度是，如果我们不知道那笔钱去哪了、为我们做了什么，我们就不愿意花一美元。很多人会假设那是一个很早的招聘——数据作为第三号招聘太早了。但我仍然觉得我们那里做对了。现在我们有了一整个数据团队，但那时我们没有。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So those were the three teams that we started with on top. And then the content person was already at Deel by the time that I joined, so that was the person I mentioned that was early employee. So that's how we originally set it.
turns.zh: 所以那是我们一开始就搭起来的三个团队（在顶层）。然后内容那个人在我加入时已经在 Deel 了，所以就是我提到的那个早期员工。所以我们最初是这么搭的。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Now the teams have changed. So now we have a different structure, slightly different structure, which is we have regional teams and functional teams. The functional teams are basically subject matter experts. They're good at what they do and we don't care where they are based in the world. So those are teams like product marketing, content, community, events, paid advertisements, brand. If we are looking for the best graphic designer in the world, I don't care where they are, they can sit wherever in the world. They are basically functional teams.
turns.zh: 现在团队变了。所以现在我们有不同的结构，略微不同的结构，就是我们有区域团队和职能团队。职能团队基本上是主题专家。他们擅长自己做的东西，我们不在乎他们在世界的哪里。所以那些团队像产品营销、内容、社区、活动、付费广告、品牌。如果我们在找世界上最好的平面设计师，我不在乎他们在哪，他们可以坐在世界的任何地方。他们基本就是职能团队。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And then we have regional teams. Because we are selling into a lot of different regions, we need to make sure that we have local expertise as well. So we have marketing managers for different key regions for us that then work with our functional teams to bring the strategy to life. So that's how we've set it.
turns.zh: 然后我们有区域团队。因为我们卖进很多不同的地区，我们需要确保也有本地专长。所以我们有针对不同关键地区的营销经理，他们再和我们的职能团队合作，把战略落地。所以我们是这么搭的。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: I've seen businesses who build out a regional team that has their own paid ads team and their own content team. But what we have found is when you take people away from their group of expertise, so if you take a paid ads person, and if you have a team of paid ads people and you separate those five people and give them to different regions, instead of letting them sit together and be a tight team, the best practice is learning and the leveling up of the skills doesn't happen as fast as they would if all of the technical roles are sitting together. So we are continuing down the road of functional and regional setup.
turns.zh: 我见过一些企业建了一个区域团队，那个团队有自己的付费广告团队和自己的内容团队。但我们发现的是，当你把人们从他们的专业群体里抽走，比如你抽一个付费广告的人，如果你有一队付费广告的人，你把那五个人分开、分给不同区域，而不是让他们坐在一起成为一个紧密的团队，最佳实践的学习和技能的提升就不会像所有技术角色坐在一起时那么快发生。所以我们继续走在职能+区域的路上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So say someone in Turkey wants to run paid ads, they convince the paid growth team to invest in resources in growing Turkey?
turns.zh: 所以假设土耳其有人想跑付费广告，他们说服付费增长团队投资资源来发展土耳其？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Exactly. So they would work with our central paid ads team to say I would like to run paid ads in Turkey, this is the audience I want to go after. And then they work together to execute on that strategy.
turns.zh: 对。所以他们会和我们的中央付费广告团队合作，说我想在土耳其跑付费广告，这是我想追的受众。然后他们一起协作执行那个战略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How does that team decide who's going to get their time, is there a rough approach to that?
turns.zh: 那个团队怎么决定谁会获得他们的时间，有没有一个大概的方法？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So it depends on the total addressable market in a region, what are the opportunities we're seeing, what's the competitive landscape like. So chances are if a market is what we consider to be tier one, and it's a place that we have seen good growth, we will invest our resources into it. And then along the way we learn and we decide if we're going to double down or pull back a little bit.
turns.zh: 这取决于一个地区的总可寻址市场、我们看到的机遇是什么、竞争态势是怎样的。所以如果一个市场是我们认为的一级市场，而且是一个我们看到良好增长的地方，我们就会把资源投进去。然后一路上我们学习，再决定是要加倍下注还是稍微收回一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I want to chat a bit about culture, culture at Deel. We had Jeff from Ramp on, and their culture is described by one word, velocity. Also one of you being the fastest growing business of all time, I'm curious how you'd contrast your culture and broadly how you think about culture at a startup and how you help create the culture at Deel?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我想聊一点文化，Deel 的文化。我们请过 Ramp 的 Jeff 来，他们的文化用一个词形容，就是 velocity（速度）。而你们俩之一也是有史以来增长最快的业务，我很好奇你会怎么对比你们的文化，以及 broadly 你怎么思考初创公司的文化、你是怎么帮着在 Deel 创造文化的？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yeah, so I would say culture is made up of two components. One is, what do you bring to the company as a team member, and what does the company give back to you? So what we expect the team members to bring to us is, our version of velocity is something that we call 'Deel speed', is that we want to make sure that we act with urgency. It doesn't matter how big the team has grown, we want to act with urgency on behalf of our customers. If a customer has a problem, they're not going to wait two weeks to get an answer for that. They're going to get that answer within 24 hours. If we need to build out a product because many customers are asking for it, that product is going to get built in one-tenth the time that any of our competitors will likely build it in.
turns.zh: 是的，所以我会说文化由两个部分组成。一个是，作为团队成员，你给公司带来什么，以及公司回馈给你什么？所以我们期望团队成员带给我们的是，我们对速度（velocity）的版本是我们称之为"Deel speed"（Deel 速度）的东西，就是我们想确保我们以紧迫感行事。不管团队长到多大，我们都要代表客户以紧迫感行事。如果一个客户有问题，他们不会等两周才得到答案。他们会在 24 小时内得到那个答案。如果因为很多客户都在要，我们需要建一个产品，那个产品的建造时间会是我们任何竞争对手可能建造它的时间的十分之一。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So 'Deel speed' is very, very important for us. And that's something we expect from our team members who are committing to it. To say, what's the quickest way I can solve this problem properly? And to repeatedly push themselves to act with urgency.
turns.zh: 所以"Deel speed"对我们来说非常重要。而那是我们期望承诺于此的团队成员带来的。去说，我能用什么最快的方式正确地解决这个问题？并反复鞭策自己以紧迫感行事。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: We also care that we remain positive. We have default optimism because we are in a new space, so if someone's going to come into Deel and they're going to be pessimistic and they're like, "I don't think that's going to work for X, Y, Z reasons," they're going to just slow things down. We need people to ask the question of, "I think it's going to work for these four reasons, now let's see what are the risks associated with it and let's seek to solve those risks." That's again something we expect from our team members.
turns.zh: 我们也看重我们保持积极。我们有"默认乐观"（default optimism），因为我们在一个新领域，所以如果有人要进 Deel，而他们悲观，像"我觉得因为 X、Y、Z 原因那不会管用"——他们只会把事情拖慢。我们需要人们问这样的问题："我觉得它会因为这四个原因管用，现在让我们看看与之相关的风险是什么，并寻求解决那些风险。"那再次是我们期望团队成员带来的。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And then the last one, well, not the last one, but one of the third important ones is, fully giving a shit about your customer. At the end of the day, the product that we have, we are dealing with humans, we're dealing with their livelihood, the way they get paid, we're dealing with the way companies hire. It's so incredibly personal if someone doesn't get their paycheck on time or if someone gets into legal trouble because their contract wasn't set up the proper way.
turns.zh: 然后最后一个——好吧，不是最后一个，但是第三个重要的之一——是，真正地在乎你的客户。说到底，我们有的这个产品，我们打交道的是人，是他们谋生的手段、他们拿到报酬的方式，我们打交道的公司招聘的方式。如果有人没按时拿到工资，或者有人因为合同没被正确设置而陷入法律麻烦，那是极其个人的事。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So recognizing that it's not a software and a platform that we're trying to make it the best, but it's like, no, it's a business trying to pay a human so they can live their lives and the business can continue growing. So that care is something that we need people to bring to the table.
turns.zh: 所以认识到我们要做好的不是一个软件和平台，而是，不，是一个试图付钱给一个人、让他们能过日子、企业能继续增长的企业。所以那种在意是我们 needs 人们带到桌面上来的。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Now in return of those things coming, what we give back as a company is, outside of obviously your pay, your benefits package, et cetera, is we offer people the flexibility to choose how and when they do their job, they get to decide on where they work from, what hours they work. So we basically give people all the freedom to set up their life how they want to as long as they come to the table giving us what they need. So I would say we do have an intense culture, and that's expected, we share that openly with people. But at the end of the day, that's also what sets us apart.
turns.zh: 现在作为这些事发生的回报，作为一家公司我们回馈的是，除了明显的你的薪水、你的福利包等等之外，是我们给人们选择如何、何时做他们工作的灵活性，他们可以决定在哪里工作、工作哪些时段。所以我们基本给人们所有自由去按他们想要的方式安排生活，只要他们来到桌前给我们所需的。所以我会说我们确实有一种高强度的文化，那是被期望的，我们公开地和人们分享这一点。但说到底，那也是我们与众不同之处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this 'Deel speed'. Are these core values basically within Deel, these are values that you come back to?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个"Deel speed"。这些核心价值基本上在 Deel 内部，是你反复回归的价值观吗？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yes, exactly. And these are values that we publicly share as well.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。而且这些也是我们公开发享的价值观。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How early in the lifecycle of the company did you all come up with these values? That's something that a lot of startups think about is, when should we actually crystallize these values?
turns.zh: 在公司生命周期的什么时候你们想出了这些价值观？很多初创公司会想这件事：我们到底什么时候应该把这些价值观固化下来？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So we came up with them, I believe it was about a year in, but we didn't sit around the table and say, "What should we call our values?" 'Deel speed' was something that our CEO would tell people. He'd be like, "Okay, I want you to do this, but I want you to do it at 'Deel speed'." And one of the early jokes was, let's have company swag that's Deel speedo and things like that. It's just like, it was already used so frequently with people that we were just like, "Okay, we keep saying this, let's also define what it actually is for us and set it in stone and share it with people." So we did go through that exercise probably about a year in into the company existing, but the culture happened well before we established that.
turns.zh: 所以我们想出它们，我相信大概是一年左右的时候，但我们不是围坐在桌子旁说"我们该怎么称呼我们的价值观？""Deel speed"是我们的 CEO 会告诉人们的东西。他会说"好，我要你做这个，但我要你用 Deel speed 来做。"早期的一个玩笑是，搞个公司周边叫 Deel speedo 之类的。就是，它已经被人们用得如此频繁，以至于我们就像"好吧，我们一直说这个，也让咱们定义一下它对我们到底是什么意思，然后把它定下来、分享给人们。"所以我们大概是在公司存在约一年时做了那个练习，但文化在我们确立它之前早就发生了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Reminds me, at Airbnb, there was a team that came up with the core values, I think it was four years in probably, and there were six of them. And then a few years later they realized two of them aren't actually true, they were aspirational. And there was this recognition that values should be who you are not who you hope to be because it just doesn't click. And so they actually cut those values and they ended up having just four values. And maybe one day they'll bring them back. And so I think that's a really good lesson is you want to see who you already are and then just represent them in a really interesting, creative way.
turns.zh: 让我想起，在 Airbnb，有一个团队想出了核心价值，我想大概是四年的时候，有六个。然后几年后他们意识到其中两个其实不是真的，它们是 aspirational（向往的）。然后有了一种认识：价值观应该是你是谁，而不是你希望成为谁，因为它就是不契合。所以他们实际上砍掉了那些价值观，最后只剩四个。也许有一天他们会再把它们拿回来。所以我觉得那是个很好的教训：你想看你已经是谁，然后用一种非常有趣、有创意的方式把它们表现出来。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yes, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a version of, what did you call it, default optimism. Airbnb's version of that was 'embrace the adventure', which is just like, this is going to be crazy, just go for it, embrace it, this is what it's going to be like.
turns.zh: 有一种版本，你叫它什么来着，默认乐观。Airbnb 的那个版本是"embrace the adventure"（拥抱冒险），就是像，这会很疯狂，去干吧，拥抱它，事情就会是那个样子。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Exactly. And try and see how can I solve this, how can this be done instead of why it won't work.
turns.zh: 没错。而且去试着看我能怎么解决这个问题、这怎么能做成，而不是为什么它不会管用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I love that. And this urgency piece comes up again and again in these interviews I'm doing. What I think of is Frank Slootman, I think is his name, the founder of Snowflake, has this book called Amp It Up. All about just how they made Snowflake work. And something he comes back to is just you need to constantly have a sense of urgency because when you don't, people get bored and they actually end up liking their job less because it's just like, I don't really know what I'm doing, things are moving along. And there's actually a lot of value in moving fast. Jeff talked about this as just like, you have less burnout when people feel like things are getting done and out the door.
turns.zh: 是的，我喜欢这个。而这个紧迫感的部分在我做的这些访谈里反复出现。我想到的是 Frank Slootman，我想是这名，Snowflake 的创始人，有本书叫 Amp It Up。全是关于他们怎么让 Snowflake 运作起来的。他反复提到的一点是，你需要持续有一种紧迫感，因为当你没有时，人们会无聊，他们实际上会更不喜欢自己的工作，因为就像，我不太知道我在做什么，事情在往前挪。而快速行动其实有很多价值。Jeff 聊过这个，就像，当人们感觉事情在被做完、在被推出门时，他们的倦怠反而更少。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yeah, it's incredibly fulfilling. I look back and sometimes things when, for example, when the SVB was going through the issues they were going through, the entire team had to work on a Sunday to communicate with our customers of like, "No, we're good, don't worry about it." But I remember that Sunday I had to miss out on a theater I was so excited to see, but it just felt like, oh my God, we're in this, it was like a war room, we're doing it. And that felt good. I didn't necessarily show up on Monday feeling already burned out, but it was more like, yes, I felt alive. And I think the right people will feel that way.
turns.zh: 是的，它极其有成就感。我回头看，有时候事情——比如当 SVB 经历他们经历的问题时，整个团队不得不在某个周日工作，和客户沟通"不，我们没事，别担心。"但我记得那个周日我错过了我超兴奋想看的一场戏，但它就是感觉，哦天哪，我们在里面，就像个作战室，我们在做。那感觉很好。我周一来的时候不一定就觉得已经倦怠了，而是更像，是的，我觉得活着。我觉得对的人会有那种感觉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and as long as it's not constantly for years just endless late nights and weekends.
turns.zh: 是的，只要它不是连续好几年不停地深夜和周末。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: It can't always be war time.
turns.zh: 不能一直是战时。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I find that those end up being the most memorable, meaningful moments is when you're working really, really hard on something that you're excited about. And it has to be something you're excited about and are proud of.
turns.zh: 我发现那些最终成为最难忘、最有意义的时刻，就是当你在为你兴奋的东西真的非常非常努力地工作时。而且它必须是你兴奋、并为之骄傲的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Last question. I saw on Twitter, you shared this photo of your home office, and it was this incredible view out the window, and then you took a photo facing your desk and it was an ironing board. And two questions there. One is just how did that all happen? And then two, I think you mentioned somewhere that you didn't even meet a lot of your coworkers for a year and a half after joining Deel, it was very remote forward. So, I'm curious also just how you made remote work work for you in that environment?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。我在 Twitter 上看到，你分享了你家庭办公室的照片，窗外是难以置信的景色，然后你拍了一张朝向你桌子的照片，是个熨衣板。两个问题。一个是，那到底是怎么发生的？第二个，我想你在哪提过，你加入 Deel 后一年半都没怎么见过很多同事，它非常向前远程。所以我也很想知道，在那个环境里你是怎么让远程工作为你所用的？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Yeah, so I'll explain the ironing board first. So that was because I was actually visiting my family in Istanbul, and in the setup that we have, there's one desk. So my husband and I go rock, paper, scissors, and we'll see who gets the desk and who gets to come up with a secondary solution. And he won the desk, so I had to come up with a creative solution. And because the view behind me was stunning, of the Bosporus, every meeting I joined, people were like, "Wow, I love your view, this is amazing." And I was like, "Oh, no, no, you guys, I'm sitting on an ironing board right now." And to me that was both funny, and I wanted to do a reality check with people to be like, "Come on, this is not as glorious as it looks." But at the same time, it really in that moment I was like, "This is awesome, I work at Deel."
turns.zh: 是的，所以先解释熨衣板。那是因为我其实是在伊斯坦布尔探望家人，而在我们的 setup 里，只有一张桌子。所以我和我丈夫猜拳，看谁得到桌子、谁得想个备选方案。他赢了桌子，所以我得想个有创意的方案。而且因为我背后是博斯普鲁斯海峡的绝美景色，我参加的每次会议，人们都会说"哇，我好爱你的景色，太棒了。"而我会说"哦不不，你们这些人，我现在是坐在一个熨衣板上。"而对我来说那既好笑，我也想和人们做个现实检查，像"拜托，这没看起来那么光彩。"但同时，在那一刻我真的想，"这太酷了，我在 Deel 工作。"

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Previously when I wanted to go visit my family in Istanbul, and I live in Canada, I would have to use my days off to go. And for me it just meant a lot to be able to do my work regardless of where I am. I had a full day of work and meetings and everything. And my work just continued and I was also be able to be with my family. So it was a moment of Deel's promise coming true in a very real way in my life. And I thought it was hilarious. My dad thought it was so unprofessional that I shared that with the public then. He hasn't fully wrapped his head around the startup world. So it was just one of those moments of sharing that, yeah, work can be remote and it can be whatever you want it to be. So that's the the story behind it. In this moment as we're recording this, I am in a proper home office with a desk and a back supported chair. It changes all the time.
turns.zh: 之前当我想去伊斯坦布尔探望家人时——我住在加拿大——我得用我的休假才能去。而对我来说，能够不管我在哪都能做我的工作，意义重大。我有满满一天的工作和会议等等。而我的工作就继续着，同时我也能和家人在一起。所以那是 Deel 的承诺在我生活中以非常真实的方式成真的一刻。而且我觉得它很滑稽。我爸当时觉得我把那个公之于众太不专业了。他还没完全搞懂初创世界。所以那只是一个分享的时刻，是的，工作可以是远程的，它可以是你想让它成为的任何样子。所以那是背后的故事。在我们录这期的此刻，我在一个正经的家庭办公室里，有桌子、有靠背支撑的椅子。它一直在变。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And in terms of, going back to your second question of, early days not meeting the team members. As I said, I joined Deel in July, 2020, pandemic was at its peak, me being based in Canada, Canada had very strict restrictions of, you can't leave the country, we won't let you back in. So I had to stay put. And I worked for a year and a half at Deel before for the first time where I met our team members was at a conference in Lisbon. And I showed up and it was this surreal moment because I've worked with them for a year and a half, we'd accomplished so much. Our revenue was already way past $50 million and I was seeing these people for the first time. So that was very funny.
turns.zh: 关于，回到你的第二个问题，早期没见过团队成员。就像我说，我 2020 年 7 月加入 Deel，疫情正盛，我 base 在加拿大，加拿大有非常严格的限制——你不能离开国家，我们也不会让你回来。所以我得待着别动。我在 Deel 工作了一年半，第一次见到我们的团队成员，是在里斯本的一个会议上。我出现时，那是个超现实的时刻，因为我已经和他们工作了一年半，我们完成了那么多。我们的收入已经远超 5000 万美元，而我第一次见到这些人。所以那很好笑。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: But if I look at the early days of Deel, there's a lot of little stories like that, where we forgot to create swag until we reached a billion dollars. And it was actually when our photo was going to be on the NASDAQ and we wanted to take a team picture that we were like, "Guys, we need to have t-shirts. Can someone please run to a store in New York and print our logo on something?" So a lot of those things just by the nature of being a pandemic business came a little bit later.
turns.zh: 但如果我看 Deel 的早期，有很多像那样的小故事，比如我们直到达到十亿估值才想起来做周边。而实际上当我们的照片要上纳斯达克、我们想拍一张团队照时，我们才像"兄弟们，我们需要 T 恤。能不能有人跑去纽约的店里，把我们的 logo 印在什么东西上？"所以很多那样的事，就因为是疫情业务的本质，来得稍微晚了一点。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: But the thing that allowed I think for me in Deel to build the culture early on was, because we all work from home, we've been like that from day one. We have the option to go into WeWorks and co-working spaces if that's something that you choose. But we all get to show up as our very authentic selves. So people have met my pets and my partner well before they would have if I was showing up to an office. So there's that sincerity that comes with being in someone's home that we really relied on early on.
turns.zh: 但我觉得让我在 Deel 早期能建立文化的东西是，因为我们都在家工作，我们从第一天起就是那样。你有选择去 WeWork 和联合办公空间，如果你选那个的话。但我们都能以最真实的自己出现。所以人们在我还没进办公室之前，就先见过了我的宠物和我的伴侣。所以那种身在某人家里的真诚感，是我们早期真的很依赖的。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And as a company, I never felt the pressure to show up in a certain way or dress up for meetings or anything. So just being able to show up as yourself, and whether you're an introverted person who never likes to turn on their camera or you're someone who's going to be like, "Here, meet my dog." That just naturally built a team culture and comradery well before we could be together in person.
turns.zh: 而作为一家公司，我从未感到要以某种方式出现、或为会议打扮什么的那种压力。所以只是能够以你自己出现，无论你是一个从不喜欢开摄像头的内向的人，还是一个会像"来，见见我的狗"的人。那就在我们能线下聚在一起之前，很自然地建立起了团队文化和战友情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Clearly it has worked out. Meltem, is there anything else that you want to share before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 显然它起作用了。Meltem，在我们进入非常激动的快问快答之前，还有什么你想分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: We had a really good conversation. The one thing I would tell people is, most of growth, people assume is very difficult. I'm not necessarily saying it's easy, but it's relatively straightforward when you go back to the first principles of just figuring out where are the people at? How can I add value? As long as your product is there to actually bring them value. So I would say people should just recognize that it's much simpler than they think it is, it just takes a lot of discipline to execute on it, it's not rocket science.
turns.zh: 我们聊得很好。我想告诉人们的一件事是，大多数人假设增长非常难。我不一定要说它容易，但当你回归第一性原理、去搞清楚人们在哪、我能怎么增加价值——只要你的产品确实能给他们带来价值——它就相对直接。所以我会说人们应该认识到它比他们想的简单得多，只是执行它需要大量纪律，它不是火箭科学。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Quite an empowering statement, I love it. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 相当赋能的一句话，我喜欢。既然如此，我们到了非常激动的快问快答环节。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: I am ready, let's do this.
turns.zh: 我准备好了，来吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你最常推荐给其他人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: From the nonfiction world, How Will You Measure Your Life by Clay Christensen, that's one I recommend. He takes the business learnings that he's had and applies it to your life. It's a very short and easy to get through book. Outside of that, I constantly recommend fiction. I think at one point it became uncool to read fiction that every moment you have needs to be productive and you need to learn something. I don't care what fiction it is you read, you can read Judy Blume for all I care, but just read fiction, be creative, do something with your brain other than reading nonfiction and learning things all the time.
turns.zh: 在非虚构世界里，Clay Christensen 的《How Will You Measure Your Life》（你将如何衡量你的人生），那是我推荐的一本。他把他的商业领悟应用到你的生活上。那是一本很短、很容易读完的书。除此之外，我不断推荐虚构作品。我觉得有段时间读虚构变得不酷了，好像你拥有的每一刻都需要有生产力、需要学到东西。我不在意你读什么虚构，你读 Judy Blume 我都无所谓，但就是去读虚构，有创意，用你的大脑做点除了读非虚构、一直学习东西之外的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've had to make that shift myself, and it's been great, but I still get drawn to nonfiction. But good reminder. What are some favorite recent movie or TV shows you've loved?
turns.zh: 我自己也得做那个转变，它很棒，但我还是会被非虚构吸引。不过很好的提醒。最近你最爱的一些电影或剧集是什么？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Favorite recent movie, I think along with everybody else, was Oppenheimer. I thought it was great. I do wish they explored a little bit more of why he was the person that drove everybody to excellence. But overall loved the movie. Did not think I could sit through three hours without peeing, but I did. And favorite recent TV show was The Summer I Turned Pretty. I absolutely love it. I don't care that it's actually designed for teenagers, I enjoyed every second of it.
turns.zh: 最近最喜欢的电影，我想和大家一样，是《奥本海默》。我觉得它很棒。我确实希望他们多探索一点，为什么他是那个把每个人都推向卓越的人。但整体爱这部电影。没想到我能坐过三小时不尿尿，但我做到了。而最近最喜欢的剧集是《The Summer I Turned Pretty》（我变漂亮的那个夏天）。我绝对爱它。我不在乎它其实是给青少年设计的，我享受它的每一秒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates when you're interviewing them?
turns.zh: 你面试候选人时喜欢问的一个 favorite 面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: What would your siblings say about you? It's very telling. If they have siblings, if they don't, I will say, what will your parents say about you? But it's very telling what you think other people think of you.
turns.zh: 你的兄弟姐妹会怎么评价你？这很能说明问题。如果他们有兄弟姐妹，如果没有，我会说，你父母会怎么评价你？但你觉得别人怎么看你，这很能说明问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you look for in their answer that gives you a sign that they're a good candidate or not?
turns.zh: 在他们的回答里你找什么，能给你信号说他们是不是个好候选人？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: I look for sincerity and self-awareness. Your siblings are never ... I mean, I love my sister, but she'll probably shit talk me a lot. And being aware of that is very important. If someone was like, "My siblings will say I'm very organized and that I'm the one that brings our family together." That's probably a bullshit answer. But if they're like, "Oh yeah, they'll say these weird things about me," that shows a little bit of self-awareness and humbleness that I want to see in a person.
turns.zh: 我找真诚和自我觉察。你的兄弟姐妹永远不会……我是说，我爱我姐，但她大概会损我很多。而意识到这一点非常重要。如果有人像"我兄弟姐妹会说我很有条理、而且我是把全家聚在一起的那个人"——那大概是个扯淡的答案。但如果他们像"哦是啊，他们会说我这些怪事"——那显示出一点我想在一个人身上看到的自我觉察和谦卑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 你最近发现、真的喜欢的一个 favorite 产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Oh, this is a dangerous one. So two, one was NuStrips, they're caffeine strips. I find caffeine pills and everything or when I drink coffee is like, accidentally I'll have 300 milligrams and then I'm buzzing. But these are 50 milligrams each, so it's very easy to stop yourself. And they don't taste bad. So those I like for when I just need a little boost.
turns.zh: 哦，这个有点危险。所以两个，一个是 NuStrips，它们是咖啡因条。我发现咖啡因药丸什么的，或者我喝咖啡时，会不小心就摄入 300 毫克，然后我就嗨了。但这些每条 50 毫克，所以很容易让自己停下。而且它们味道不差。所以那些是我想要点小 boost 时喜欢的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So they're just strips that you put in your mouth and they give you caffeine?
turns.zh: 所以它们就是放进嘴里的条、给你咖啡因？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Like LISTERINE strips.
turns.zh: 像 LISTERINE 条那样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What?
turns.zh: 什么？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And you put it on your tongue and then it also doesn't give you the jitters and it's just 50 milligrams, which is a very mild cup of coffee.
turns.zh: 你把它放舌头上，然后它也不给你 jitter（手抖心慌），就 50 毫克，是一杯非常温和的咖啡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Microdosing caffeine.
turns.zh: 微量摄入咖啡因。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Beautiful.
turns.zh: 美。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: And the second one is, I recently was gifted a personalized library stamp, which I love. Because I love to give books away, so I stamp them with my library stamp. And I like to think that one day in a secondhand bookshop I'm going to run into it.
turns.zh: 第二个是，我最近被送了一个个性化的藏书印章，我喜欢。因为我喜欢送书，所以我就用我的藏书印章盖章。而且我喜欢想，有一天在一家二手书店里我会碰到它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing. There's a camp at Burning Man that's a library, and you can borrow books and you have to return it in a year, the next year when you come back to Burning Man. Which is amazing. And then there's a guy that has a megaphone, he is just like, "A book has been returned." Makes a whole scene about it. What is a favorite life motto that you often come back to or share with other people, either at work or in life?
turns.zh: 那太棒了。Burning Man 有一个营地是图书馆，你可以借书，而且你得在一年后的明年你回到 Burning Man 时还回来。那很棒。然后有个拿着扩音器的人，他就像"一本书被还回来了。"搞出好大一场面。你经常回归、或和别人分享的一个 favorite 人生格言是什么，无论在工作还是生活里？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: The world is run by insecure overachievers. I used to think my insecurity was a downfall and I would just hide it and try to pretend it's not there. And then someone that I really look up to told that to. I'm like, "Okay, so I'm not the only one." And it's just, I do think world is run by a bunch of people that have something to prove for a good reason or not, but it's better to embrace it than to pretend you're all confident and you're just doing this because you're brilliant.
turns.zh: 这个世界是由不安全的 overachiever（过度成就者）运行的。我以前觉得我的不安全感是个弱点，我会藏起它、假装它不在。然后一个我真的很仰望的人告诉我那个。我会想"好吧，所以我不孤单。"而且它就是这样，我确实觉得世界是由一群有东西要证明的人运行的，不管有没有好理由，但拥抱它比假装你全都很自信、你做这个只是因为你很杰出要好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God, so good. Final question, what is your favorite Canadian food? You live in Canada and thus the question.
turns.zh: 哦天哪，太好了。最后一个问题，你最喜欢的加拿大食物是什么？你住在加拿大，所以这个问题。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Okay, it's not particularly food, but Caesars, they're basically Bloody Mary's with clam juice.
turns.zh: 好的，它不特别是食物，但 Caesars（恺撒鸡尾酒），它们基本就是加了蛤蜊汁的血腥玛丽。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, Bloody Caesar, is that what they're called? Or just Caesar?
turns.zh: 哦，Bloody Caesar，它们叫那个吗？还是就叫 Caesar？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: They're called Caesars.
turns.zh: 它们叫 Caesars。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just Caesar.
turns.zh: 就 Caesar。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: But the American equivalent would be a Bloody Mary. It's so much better than a Bloody Mary. It's not vegan. And then the reason I qualify it as food is when you order it in Canada, it comes with pepperoni strips and pickled asparagus, and they'll shove a whole meal in there. And it's just amazing and something that America should definitely adapt too.
turns.zh: 但美国的等价物会是 Blood Mary。它比血腥玛丽好太多了。它不是素食。而我把它归类为食物的原因是，你在加拿大点它时，它会配着意大利辣香肠条和腌芦笋上来，他们会把一整顿饭塞进去。它就是惊人，而且是美国绝对也应该采用的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think I've had one, I think I prefer Bloody Marys, but a good pitch for the Caesars. Meltem, thank you so much for being here. We talked about growth strategy, team building, 'Deel speed', default optimism, so many things. Really appreciate you making the time. Two final questions, where can folks find you online if they want to reach out? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 我想我喝过一次，我想我更喜欢血腥玛丽，但为 Caesars 做了个好 pitch。Meltem，非常感谢你能来。我们聊了增长战略、团队建设、"Deel speed"、默认乐观，好多东西。真的很感激你抽时间。最后两个问题，如果人们想联系，能在哪里网上找到你？以及听众怎么能对你有用的？

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: So they can reach out to me on Twitter at MeltemK, I'm the fastest to respond there. Please don't reach out to me on LinkedIn, I never respond there. And the way readers can be useful to me is if they, one, we're always looking for feedback on Deel. If you see something out there that you think could be better, let me know, and I'll make sure to communicate it to the team, whatever that may be. And also, if anybody has tips that they think I would benefit from or any good fiction book recommendations, I'm always open to them.
turns.zh: 所以他们可以在 Twitter 上 @MeltemK 联系我，我在那里回得最快。请别在 LinkedIn 上联系我，我从来不在那回。而读者能对我有用的方式是，第一，我们一直在找对 Deel 的反馈。如果你在外面看到你觉得能更好的东西，让我知道，我会确保把它传达给团队，不管那是什么。还有，如果任何人有他们认为我会受益的 tips、或任何好的虚构书推荐，我一直都开放。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Meltem, thank you again so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。Meltem，再次非常感谢你能来。

turns.speaker: Meltem Kuran Berkowitz
turns.en: Thank you so much for having me.
turns.zh: 非常感谢你邀请我。
